Title: Digital Transformation and Green Total Factor Productivity in China
Authors: Junbing Huang, Wanrui He, Yajun Wang, Yimin Lu
Affiliations: School of Economics Southwestern University of Finance and Economics Chengdu China; School of Digital Economics and Management Wuxi University Wuxi China; Department of Economics, Business School Nanjing University Nanjing China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Achieving sustainable development relies on the continuous improvement of green total factor productivity (GTFP). Although existing studies have documented a positive association between digital transformation and GTFP through technological innovation, the underlying mechanism remains insufficiently understood because technological innovation is often treated as an aggregate channel. Such aggregate treatments are ineffective in clarifying the underlying mechanisms of action within it and carrying out targeted policy. In this paper, we open this black box by dividing the technology innovation caused by digitization into indigenous R&D efficiency improvement and technology spillovers increase. Through a dataset covering China's A‐share listed enterprises over the period 2012–2021, together with the Global Malmquist‐Luenberger index based on a super‐efficiency Slacks‐Based Measure model and econometric analysis, we show that digitization significantly enhances GTFP. More importantly, the increases in both indigenous R&D efficiency and technology spillovers coming from digital transformation are two important channels to promote GTFP. Our study offers insights for emerging economies aiming to achieve green growth through digital reforms.

Title: Factors influencing drug diffusion: a practical guide to the use of medicare part D claims
Authors: Yuchen Wang, Giedre Kvedaraviciene, Phillip Phan
Abstract: Because of the methods by which they are produced, drugs embody technical knowledge and are the subject of technology transfer strategies among biopharmaceutical companies. Additionally, drug diffusion shapes the structure of the biopharmaceutical industry, the sustainability of pharmaceutical markets, and patient outcomes. This article provides a practical guide to using Medicare Part D Prescription Drug Event (PDE) data to model and analyze the factors and dynamics that drive drug diffusion. Medicare accounts for approximately a third of total U.S. prescription drug spending and covers more than 56 million beneficiaries, making it the most representative dataset of the U.S. older adult population and people with disabilities. The PDE’s strengths include national representativeness, detailed transactional data, and the capacity for longitudinal and multilevel analyses. Its limitations include the absence of diagnostic detail, the reporting of list rather than net prices, and limited generalizability to non-Medicare populations. The complementary use of other data sources can mitigate these weaknesses. Hence, we describe linkage strategies that integrate PDE claims with the Medicare Beneficiary Summary File, the Prescriber Characteristics File, outpatient claims, and external data sources, including FDA approval data and U.S. Census indicators. Particular attention is given to handling many-to-many linkages and to constructing analytic datasets that preserve contextual validity. We demonstrate how researchers can evaluate the roles of patient demographics, comorbidities, prescriber attributes, and formulary design in shaping drug diffusion. We argue that Medicare Part D claims data provide a uniquely powerful platform for studying technology transfer and innovation diffusion in an industrial sector that accounts for 20% of the U.S. economy.

Title: Short-run pain, long-term gain? R&D investment and firm growth in Indian pharma
Authors: Rosa Cocozza, Serena Gallo, Amith V. Megaravalli, Vincenzo Verdoliva
Abstract: This paper examines whether R&D investment enhances firm growth and profitability in the Indian pharmaceutical industry, with particular attention to capability thresholds, heterogeneity, and peer spillovers. Using an unbalanced panel of 195 listed pharmaceutical firms from 2012 to 2024, we estimate fixed-effects regressions, propensity score matching, and quantile regressions to assess the impact of R&D intensity and adoption on sales growth and profitability, while accounting for firm heterogeneity and selection bias. Results show that firms with higher R&D investment tend to experience lower short-run growth but stronger long-run growth, consistent with the delayed innovation payoffs. Investment intensity consistently supports growth, whereas profitability and leverage do not mitigate short-run R&D adjustment costs. Peer R&D exposure generates modest spillover benefits, and heterogeneity analysis indicates that fast-growing firms are better able to absorb R&D costs. This study provides novel firm-level evidence on R&D payoffs in the Indian pharmaceutical sector during the post-TRIPS and post-demonetization period, extending prior OECD-based evidence to an emerging-market context.

Title: How technological path of internationalization matters? A dynamic capability perspective
Authors: Zhen Wang
Abstract: Internationalizing technology operations early are widely regarded as important antecedents to superior growth among international new ventures (INVs). Yet, while studies have examined the effects of technological position on INV growth, a dynamic perspective is still missing. Taking a perspective of dynamic capability theory, I shed light on the effect of heterogeneity in technology path on INV growth in terms of a curvilinear relationship. How do dynamic technological path matter for INV growth? To address this question, I introduce and measure for the first time a concept of internationalization technological path heterogeneity to capture the path-specific feature for INVs’ technological capability building, on panel data from 160 INVs. The results shows that technological path heterogeneity play a significant role in driving the growth of INVs.

Title: Facilitating corporate patent transactions: the effect of director networks and the moderating role of technological competition
Authors: Lulu Lin, Huaqi Chai, Xiaodong Geng, Wenbo Jiang
Abstract: Based on resource dependence theory and social network theory, this study examines the impact of two types of director network structures on corporate patent transactions and their boundary conditions using a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2007 to 2023. First, we find that the centrality of the director network significantly promotes patent purchases, while structural holes exhibit a U-shaped effect on patent purchases. Second, both network centrality and structural holes positively influence patent sales. Third, we further explore the moderating mechanisms by which director networks affect firms’ patent transactions. Specifically, in terms of patent purchases, technological competition negatively moderates the positive relationship between the centrality of the director network and patent purchases while positively moderating the U-shaped relationship between structural holes and patent purchases. In terms of patent sales, technological competition negatively moderates the positive effects of network centrality on patent sales, yet it cannot moderate the positive effect of structural holes on patent sales. This paper enriches the research on expanding corporate patent trading partners through director networks. The findings provide some references for firms to optimize patent transaction strategies.

Title: Fostering economic growth and convergence: assessing the impact of innovation on county disparities in the United States
Authors: Hannah E. Richards, Spencer A. Yasar
Abstract: This study examines the impact of latent innovation on the growth and convergence of economic outcomes across United States (U.S.) counties from 2005 to 2020. We find that counties with lower initial gross domestic product (GDP) experience increased growth, and this growth accelerates with higher overall levels of innovation, with initial GDP and GDP growth both relative to the frontier of New York County. Additionally, we investigate innovation arising from supplier transactions (process innovation) and supplier transactions (product innovation). Our results are consistent for both process and product innovation, though we find that process innovation has a greater impact on growth and convergence than product innovation. These findings remain robust against endogeneity due to unobserved variables. Our research demonstrates that innovation influences economic development even at the granular level of U.S. counties. This can motivate policymakers to foster a local environment that encourages innovation and, consequently, economic growth.

Title: The impact of technology transfer on industrial upgrading in China: an analysis based on patent data
Authors: Yujiao Xian, Min Hu, Suping Peng, Mei Song
Abstract: As a major technological power, technology transfer (TT) is crucial to China’s industrial upgrading and high-quality economic development. Based on 127,586 patent data from 25 high-innovation economies over 2003–2023, this study develops an integrated framework to analyze the impact of TT on industrial upgrading in China. We first estimate the effectiveness of technology transfer-out (TT-out) and transfer-in (TT-in) in China. TT-out denotes domestic-originated patents exported from Chinese entities to international recipients, while TT-in indicates patent applications originating from foreign entities legally transferred to Chinese recipients. Then, we apply fixed-effect and threshold effect models to elucidate TT-driven mechanisms for China’s industrial technology and structure upgrading. Results indicate that (i) there are cyclical fluctuations in the effectiveness of TT-out and TT-in during 2003–2023, with values ranging from 0.028 to 0.102 and 0.049 to 0.125, respectively. (ii) TT-in and TT-out both significantly drive China’s industrial technology and structure upgrading at 1% significance level. A one-unit increase in TT-out corresponds to a 0.873-unit advancement in technological upgrading and a 0.143-unit gain in structural upgrading, while each unit rise in TT-in drives a 0.684-unit improvement in technological upgrading and a 0.050-unit enhancement in structural upgrading. (iii) Threshold effect models further demonstrate nonlinear relationships between TT and industrial upgrading, moderated by indigenous innovation input, imitative innovation input, and technology absorption capacity.

Title: Research on the impact of policy tool combinations on digital technology R&D alliances in complex network environments
Authors: Neng Shen, Jing Zhang, Yangchun Cao, Lianjun Wu
Abstract: Policy tools serve as critical instruments for promoting the diffusion of digital technology R&D alliances. However, there remains a lack of in-depth analysis regarding the combined effects and dynamic revenue of these policy tools. Based on the complex network evolution game model, this study systematically investigates the comprehensive impact of various policy tool combinations on digital technology R&D alliances, innovatively integrating the rule-based context of the dynamic revenue mechanism. The findings reveal that individual policies can all play positive roles in fostering digital technology R&D alliances. Nevertheless, the combined effects of policy tools vary, leading to heterogeneous outcomes such as enhancement, weakening, or even reversal. Under the dynamic revenue mechanism, factors such as innovation dividend factor, opportunity loss factor and revenue influence cycle exhibit positive promoting effects. Conversely, the scale of the network may exert adverse effects when it becomes excessively large. This research broadens the analytical perspective of digital technology R&D alliances by considering the combination of policy tools and the dynamic revenue mechanism, thereby proposing corresponding strategies that can provide optimization insights for both enterprise alliance strategies and government management mechanisms in the realm of digital technology R&D.

Title: University–industry interaction and firms’ innovation performance: new evidence from the biopharmaceutical industry
Authors: Anna Giunta, Eleonora Pierucci, Davide Vurchio
Abstract: Abstract This study examines the impact of university-industry (U-I) interaction on firms’ innovation performance in the biopharmaceutical industry, focusing on understanding the temporal relationship between co-publishing and innovation. Using a sample of Italian biopharmaceutical firms from 2000 to 2010, we explore whether collaborative research, specifically co-publishing between public and private research entities, influences firms’ likelihood of innovation and the intensity of their innovation activities. Our investigation sheds light on the temporal aspects of the knowledge generation process and its implications for firms’ innovation endeavours. It reveals an “anticipatory effect” of co-publishing on innovation outcomes. Our findings, corroborated by a set of robustness checks, detect that the influence of collaboration on innovation activities precedes the appearance of a joint publication, ruling out the hypothesis of “defensive publication” as a complementary part of a firm’s overall IP protection strategy pursued by biopharmaceutical firms.

Title: The role of traceability technologies in the sustainable evolution of the luxury industry
Authors: Martine Hlady-Rispal, Benjamin Adam, Christina Theodoraki, Vincent Jolivet
Abstract: In the emerging literature on the role of traceability technologies in corporate sustainability, the context of luxury products remains underexplored. This study draws on value theory to examine the role of traceability and its potential to shape the sustainable evolution of the French leather luxury industry across its supply chain (SC). Adopting a qualitative approach combining analysis of luxury brands’ CSR reports with longitudinal interviews, the study examines the complexity of the leather SC and traceability practices across a diverse range of luxury stakeholders. The results indicate that traceability is not inherently linked to sustainability, yet it can address emerging sustainability challenges and support the transformation of a complex luxury industry. Moreover, the scope, benefits and knowledge spillovers identified require extensive collaboration across all levels of the supply chain, which can be difficult to achieve in practice. The findings also underscore the importance of aligning traceability with technological, strategic, and relational dimensions to create value and foster the development of sustainable SCs.

Title: Bridging digital transformation and green innovation in firms: a dual-dimensional analysis of disclosure-behavior alignment
Authors: Yue Yang, Fan Luo
Abstract: Digital transformation (DT) has emerged as a critical catalyst for corporate sustainable development, wherein the alignment between DT disclosure and actual behavior plays a vital role in shaping organizational credibility and determining the effectiveness of its green innovation (GI) outcomes. Utilizing data from China’s A-share listed companies spanning 2010 to 2022, this study investigates how DT disclosure-behavior congruence influences corporate GI. The results reveal that a “high disclosure–high behavior” (HDHB) digital transformation, characterized by strong alignment between rhetorical commitments and concrete actions, substantially enhances the quantity and quality of GI. These positive effects are especially pronounced under conditions of heightened economic policy uncertainty, stringent regional intellectual property protection, and within technology-intensive industries. The mechanism analysis identifies three primary channels through which HDHB digital transformation facilitates GI, namely by enhancing information transparency, improving investment efficiency, and strengthening corporate social responsibility awareness. A quadrant-based analysis further indicates that while both DT disclosure and behavior independently support GI, their alignment in the HDHB configuration delivers the most substantial benefits, whereas other configurations yield more limited or inconsistent effects. This study contributes novel empirical evidence on how strategic alignment between DT disclosure and behavior functions as an effective governance mechanism, enabling firms to better translate digital transformation efforts into sustainable innovation outcomes. It also offers policy insights for promoting standardized corporate disclosure and fostering innovation-driven green development.

Title: The Bell inequality: applying the lessons of compulsory licensing to AI/ML and the Big 5
Authors: Antonio Llopis, Nicholas Vonortas
Abstract: Silicon Valley is viewed as an exemplar of rapid progress and innovation, but the US Government’s role in its origins is often overlooked. In 1956, as a result of anti-competitive behavior, Bell Corporation entered into a consent decree with the Department of Justice which enforced compulsory licensing of all its patents. This licensing led to a dramatic change in the dynamics around the development of the transistor, resulting in an era of growth and innovation that fundamentally altered the world and established the US’s dominance in computing and high-tech industries. Today, the situation with artificial intelligence parallels that of the transistor, with the Big 5 technology companies—Alphabet/Google, Apple, Meta/Facebook, Microsoft and Amazon—playing the role of the Bell System in controlling patents surrounding the technology and engaging in similar anti-competitive behavior. This paper serves as an exploration of major questions surrounding Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML), innovation and the Big 5. In this paper we: explore how AI/ML differs from other general purpose technologies (GPT); discuss why AI/ML, as a nascent GPT needs additional protection; and discuss why applying compulsory licensing of artificial intelligence patents on the Big 5 may be essential for ensuring that the US economy reaps the rewards of the coming technological boom. We draw parallels between Bell’s behavior and that of the Big 5 today, including their anti-competitive behaviors, argue that compulsory licensing of the Big 5’s AI intellectual property can be the appropriate remedy, and examine the risks and benefits of enacting such measures.

Title: Struggling with entrepreneurial ecosystems
Authors: Michael Fritsch
Abstract: Abstract This article discusses the notion of entrepreneurial ecosystems and proposes directions for the further development of the concept. Since the main goal of the concept is to identify factors that determine regional development, the key variable to assess the quality of an EE and the effect of respective policy measures should be a measure of regional performance. It is argued that a broad definition of entrepreneurship should be applied that includes the entire universe of new businesses (‘everyday’ entrepreneurship), and also accounts for incumbent firms. There is good reason to regard EE as a part of the regional innovation system and merge the two concepts. The paper discusses a number of open questions concerning the elements of a system and its dynamic properties. Finally, it outlines several key challenges for the further development of the concept.

Title: The impact of cumulative experience and R&D investment on technological change amid uncertainty in technological learning
Authors: Shiguo Zhou, Yaru Zhang
Abstract: This study constructs a two-factor technology adoption model that integrates uncertainty in technology learning by incorporating learning-by-doing (LBD) for cumulative experience and learning-by-searching (LBS) for research and development (R&D) investment. It uses the model to focus on the impact of uncertainty in the two types of technology learning (LBD and LBS) on the diffusion trend of emerging technologies. The main findings of this study are as follows: (1) Factors such as high learning rates, low initial investment costs, high carbon taxes, low uncertainty in learning rates, high risk tolerance, and high demand may promote the adoption and widespread deployment of emerging energy technologies. (2) The sensitivity of technology diffusion to changes in technology learning rates is highly non-linear, particularly when influenced by the LBD learning effect. This indicates that the tendency toward technology diffusion is affected more by cumulative experience than by R&D investment. (3) Accumulated experience is more sensitive to uncertainty than R&D investment.

Title: The business of supporting open innovation: drivers of value capture of business incubators across German regions
Authors: Adrian Toroslu, Brita Schemmann, Maryse M.H. Chappin, Carolina Castaldi, Andrea M. Herrmann
Abstract: Abstract Business incubators (BIs) play a crucial role in fostering entrepreneurship and regional innovation. However, while considerable attention has been given to their positive impact on tenants, little is known about how BIs capture value from offering their services. Drawing on the open innovation framework and regional innovation systems literature, this research investigates the relationship between internal and external openness of BIs and their ability to capture value, considering the influence of regional knowledge resources on this relationship. We tested our hypotheses on a sample of 109 German BIs, collecting data from a survey of their managers and from regional data sources. Our findings suggest that fostering internal networking among tenants is positively associated with BIs’ value capture, emphasizing the importance of facilitating knowledge exchange within incubator environments. Surprisingly, external openness was not related to BI value capture. Moreover, we identify a negative moderation effect of regional private knowledge levels on the relationship between external openness and BI value capture. These findings bear implications for research and practice alike.

Title: Cluster and local science-industry collaborations: evidence from a place-based innovation policy
Authors: Aurelien Quignon
Abstract: Place-based cluster policies have been widely adopted to foster regional innovation by promoting R&D collaborations. While previous research highlights the behavioral additionality of these policies, evidence regarding their effectiveness in fostering science-industry (S-I) collaborations remains limited. This paper examines the impact of the establishment of the French Competitive Cluster Program in 2005 on S-I collaborations. Leveraging a novel dataset of collaborative patents from 2000 to 2018, the results show that the cluster policy increases S-I collaborations within targeted regions. Additional analyses suggest that the effect is strongest in knowledge-intensive sectors and is associated with higher patent quality. Furthermore, the cluster policy induces a shift in innovative search strategies, with greater reliance on prior knowledge, suggesting a move toward incremental innovation. The findings contribute to the literature on the effectiveness of place-based cluster policies on science-industry collaborations and offer new insights into how to promote new collaborations through direct R&D subsidies and the diffusion of academic research into industrial applications.

Title: Innovation culture, technology transfer & performance: An empirical examination of the U.S. Department of Energy National Laboratories
Authors: C. Brooke Dobni, Jason Stolworthy, Grant Alexander Wilson, Tyler Case, James P. Keating
Abstract: To date, innovation culture and performance research has been conducted with heterogeneous samples of for-profit private or publicly traded firms. Limited research has examined the innovation culture and performance relationship among not-for-profit organizations, much less in government organizations with homogeneous resources and strategies. This study advances innovation culture and performance research, as it examines a mediator, technology transfer, among a sample of the U.S. Department of Energy’s National Laboratories. The results show that innovation culture differed among the National Laboratories and had positive direct and indirect effects, via technology transfer, on performance measured by technology-related key performance indicators. This suggests that, all else being equal (resources and strategies), an innovation culture can be the “difference-maker” in achieving key performance indicators. Additionally, an innovation culture can foster technology transfer that also improves key performance indicators. The research offers important contributions to innovation culture research and managerial implications for practitioners seeking to improve organizational outcomes.

Title: The role of research and other inputs for the development and impacts of standards
Authors: Knut Blind, Luzie Kromer
Abstract: Abstract Research as input into standardisation processes is becoming more important because of its role as a knowledge and technology transfer channel. Furthermore, standards have to become more science-based, particularly if they are part of the regulatory framework, such as in the European Union. Therefore, a conceptual model of standardisation as a channel of technology transfer has been expanded further to consider standards in the regulatory framework. The empirical study aims to identify the demands of industry and other stakeholders for standards as potential research results and other drivers and inputs. A survey among over thirty thousand experts active in the German standardisation body DIN generated almost three thousand responses, mainly from the industry. The responses from the experts reveal that policy initiatives, including regulations and customer requirements, alongside own and collaborative research, are the most relevant sources for standard development. Research input is assessed to be most important for measurement and testing standards, with quality and environmental standards closely followed. The primary benefit of utilizing research as input for standardisation is free access to scientific insights and the capability to stay updated with scientific advancements. Eventually, we correlate the relevance of inputs into standards by assessing various impact dimensions, revealing significant linkages. Finally, we link the empirical findings to the presented model and derive avenues for future theory-building research.

Title: Innovation prizes as a novel approach to university technology transfer: insights from the 2004–2007 DARPA Grand Challenges
Authors: Andrew Hanus, Christopher S. Hayter
Abstract: Abstract Although innovation prizes are increasingly recognized for their ability to catalyze technological advancement, stimulate public engagement, and foster the formation of technical communities, their role in university technology transfer remains underexplored. To address this gap, we examine the 2004–2007 DARPA Grand Challenges (DGCs) as an illustrative case. Based on an eight-year inductive investigation, we find that the DGCs accelerated the dissemination, development, and commercialization of robotics technologies rooted in publicly funded research by attracting diverse participants, fostering novel collaborations, and emphasizing real-world performance over formalized IP protection. In contrast to linear, patent-centric models of technology transfer, the DGCs catalyzed two-way knowledge flows between universities and external actors—including industry professionals, entrepreneurs, and hobbyists—while reinforcing core university missions of research, education, and public engagement, thereby generating broader public value. The competitions also leveraged broader policy and technological trends, such as enabling technologies and supportive prize legislation, illustrating how contextual factors shape when and how prizes complement traditional transfer mechanisms. In doing so, this study underscores the value of innovation prizes as an important complement to linear approaches and advances understanding of alternative pathways for university technology transfer.

Title: Launching lean: insights from early-stage entrepreneurship development programs for scientists
Authors: Christopher S. Hayter, Jonathan Merker, Tennille Eyre, Alan C. O’Connor
Abstract: Abstract University-based technology commercialization is widely recognized as a key driver of economic development, prompting extensive research into support programs—such as venture funds, accelerators, and proof-of-concept centers—designed to support academic entrepreneurship. Yet, many university scientists lack the entrepreneurial skills, experience, and networks required to navigate commercialization pathways effectively. In response, a new generation of government-supported programs has emerged globally, with a primary focus on early-stage entrepreneurial development. This study examines the origins, design, and evolution of such initiatives across eight countries, most of which are modeled on the U.S. National Science Foundation’s Innovation Corps (I-Corps) program but have been adapted to reflect regional contexts and institutional needs. Through cross-case analysis, we demonstrate that these programs constitute a multi-tiered infrastructure that strengthens the translation of academic research into market-ready innovations. These initiatives are increasingly vital to the advancement of entrepreneurial universities and the maturation of national and regional innovation ecosystems. The paper concludes with comparative insights and suggestions for future research. For policymakers and program designers, the findings highlight how program choices can be used as levers to strengthen entrepreneurial capacity, align interventions with the diverse needs of scientists, and improve the integration of customer discovery and related forms of training withing broader ecosystems.

Title: Revealing the impact of technological niche on value co-creation: the moderating role of the open innovation ecosystem structure
Authors: Hongwei Wang, Xuemei Xie
Abstract: Organizations have been endeavoring to establish or integrate into open innovation ecosystems (OIEs) to achieve value co-creation with their components efficiently due to the development of a global value system. However, empirical research on the factors influencing value co-creation within OIEs remains limited. Therefore, this study proposes a conceptual framework for examining the relationship between technological niche and value co-creation within OIEs. Using a dataset of 397 listed biopharmaceutical enterprises from 2012 to 2020, we find that technological niche has a significant positive effect on value co-creation within OIEs. Further, the component interdependence within OIEs exhibits a U-shaped moderation effect on the relationship between the technological niche and value co-creation. In contrast, the component status dispersion demonstrates an inverted U-shaped moderation effect on this relationship. Overall, this research provides a clearer understanding of how OIEs realize value co-creation by analyzing the influencing factors from the technological niche perspective and examining the contingent factors from the ecosystem structure perspective.

Title: Knowledge co-creation in innovation ecosystems and breakthrough innovation: the contradictory roles of capability reconfiguration
Authors: Yi Jin, Bo Liu
Abstract: Firms may benefit from knowledge co-creation in the innovation ecosystem, causing the innovation ecosystem to serve as an efficient way to generate breakthrough innovation. However, the in-and-out ways of knowledge co-creation in the ecosystem have not been fully explored collectively. Drawing on knowledge-based view and dynamic capability theory, we categorize two types of knowledge co-creation between the focal firm and ecosystem partners, namely embedded knowledge co-creation and alliance knowledge co-creation. Thereafter, we link knowledge co-creation and breakthrough innovation of the focal firm and further analyze the mediating role of capability reconfiguration. An empirical examination of 382 surveys from Chinese high-tech firms reveals that both two types of knowledge co-creation can promote breakthrough innovation. Besides, substitutional capability significantly mediates the relationships between knowledge co-creation and breakthrough innovation, while evolutionary capability reconfiguration suppresses the above relationships. Our findings extend the context of knowledge co-creation to innovation ecosystems and contributes to innovation and dynamic capability literature. Our study also expounds on valuable practical implications for managers.

Title: Agglomeration and spillovers: concentration versus dispersion. Evidence from regional innovative startups in Italy
Authors: Gustavo Barboza, Alessandro Braga
Abstract: Abstract Tracking more than 9000 Italian innovative start-ups geocoded at the one-kilometer resolution, we deploy a multilevel space–time model, instrumented with historical road networks, to examine how regional ecosystems shape entrepreneurial concentration. We revisit the three classical Marshallian channels (specialization, competition, and labor pooling), and we test asymmetric, cross-border knowledge spillovers and show that agglomeration can either amplify or dilute technology transfer across neighboring territories. Our results reveal sharp regional–sector asymmetries: some pairs intensify clustering while others next door disperse, exposing hidden dynamics that uniform models overlook. By reframing agglomeration as both conduit and barrier to technology transfer, we demonstrate that firm intensity depends not only on local Marshallian forces but also on the relative stocks of high-skilled human capital that mediates “push” and “pull” spillovers along shared borders. Sector-level decomposition further indicates that manufacturing and knowledge-intensive services respond differently to diversity and specialization, challenging one-size-fits-all prescriptions. Because identical policy levers yield divergent outcomes, the implications of this study suggest that policymakers need to be well aware that agglomeration is industry-sector-specific and conditional on the existing level of industry development already existing in each location. Therefore, place-sensitive policies in specific regional corridors accounting for industry mix and existing agglomeration levels should be the approach to follow for designing regional economic policy. We position cross-border technology transfer as the missing link reconciling the long-standing debate between concentration and dispersion strategies, providing a roadmap for place-based innovation policy.

Title: Exploring the research landscape and theoretical frameworks of enterprise scientific capability: a bibliometric investigation
Authors: Weijie Zhu, Wucheng Han, Ruoyu Lu
Abstract: With the rapid development of emerging industries, the role of science as a driving force has become increasingly prominent. An increasing number of enterprises are engaging in scientific research, cultivating and strengthening their scientific capabilities, which are critical for achieving core competitive advantages and driving technological breakthroughs in their industries. However, current academic research on enterprise scientific capability (ESC) remains fragmented and underdeveloped, lacking a unified discourse and systematic theoretical foundation. This study, grounded in enterprise capability theory and knowledge management theory, employs the CiteSpace software to conduct a systematic bibliometric analysis of literature related to enterprises and science activities. Through an extensive literature review, the study categorizes ESC into five sub-dimensions: Independent Scientific Capability (ISC), Collaborative Scientific Capability (CSC), Scientific Network Capability (NSC), Scientific Search Capability (SSC), and Scientific Absorptive Capability (ASC). Through an in-depth bibliometric and qualitative review, this research analyzes the key antecedents and influence mechanisms associated with each dimension, thereby uncovering how ESC contributes to enterprises’ knowledge accumulation, innovation performance, and commercial success. Moreover, the study outlines a clear research agenda for advancing future ESC studies. By bridging fragmented scholarship and integrating knowledge management and capability theories, this research significantly extends Teece’s enterprise capability framework. It not only lays a solid theoretical foundation for the emerging field of ESC but also provides actionable insights for enterprises seeking to enhance their scientific engagement and strategic innovation capacity.

Title: Nurturing the sustainable and circular economy: an integrated ecosystems model
Authors: João J. Ferreira, Cristina I. Fernandes, Pedro Mota Veiga, Lawrence Dooley
Abstract: This research investigates factors contributing to the transition towards green innovations. The study employed a four-study research design to achieve a holistic understanding across the multiple levels of the ecosystem. Firstly, a systematic literature review is conducted to develop a conceptual model for identifying variables to nurture transition (study 1) across the ecosystem layers. Secondly, micro-level analysis examines the strategic orientations (market and product) that impact companies' green innovations (study 2). Thirdly, meso-level analysis identifies the moderating effect of industry type on the relationship between strategic orientations and green innovations (study 3), and the final study evaluates the impact of environmental assets on economic growth and the mediating role of Industry 4.0 on this relationship (study 4). The development and testing of the multi-level model contribute to this emerging field, reflecting the integrated nature of ecosystems and identifying advantageous strategies for nurturing ecosystem transition towards increased sustainable and circular economies. Our results highlight the evidence on the relationship between environmental asset management and economic growth. This shows the importance of technology transfer in this context cannot be underestimated. This multi-level model, developed through systematising the different theories of this field of study, contributes not only by illuminating the inter-relationship across these multiple levels of the ecosystem but also by providing quantitative analysis of the key macro, meso, and micro variables that will nurture transition to ecosystem circularity.

Title: Impact of entrepreneurship education and university ecosystem on graduate entrepreneurship
Authors: Matías Lira, Maribel Guerrero
Abstract: Universities have been drivers of entrepreneurship and innovation through commercialized knowledge, the development of human capital, the launch of entrepreneurial initiatives, and participation in collaborative initiatives with local, regional, and international partners. Consequently, universities have developed multiple mechanisms to foster entrepreneurship and innovation through various educational programs and infrastructure. It also explains why universities have been socially encouraged to create new learning models that align with generational desires and employers’ requirements, as well as enrich the entrepreneurial culture through multiple initiatives. Although the literature on university entrepreneurship continues to expand, re-thinking the configuration of a combined entrepreneurship education and university entrepreneurship ecosystems strategy oriented towards generating multiple impacts on the university community still demands conceptual and empirical discussion. This paper examines the influence of entrepreneurship education (EE) and a university entrepreneurial ecosystem (UEE) on graduates´ entrepreneurship. Our results capture the specific influence of entrepreneurship education, as well as the influence of university ecosystem mechanisms on graduates’ entrepreneurial actions by extending the academic debate about the metrics and effectiveness of entrepreneurship education and the university ecosystem.

Title: Innovation activities in developing countries: the case of Bangladesh and Malaysia
Authors: Md Rashedur Rahman Sardar, Martijn van Hasselt
Abstract: Abstract Innovation is crucial for a country’s economic growth and development. It stimulates productivity and enhances the competitiveness of firms, universities, and other research institutions. Research and development (R&D) investments are one of the most significant inputs to a firm’s ability to innovate. Studies of firms in developed countries have validated the R&D-to-innovation relationship; however, there remains a void in the literature of studies focusing on the R&D-to-innovation relationship in developing countries. This paper explores the effect of R&D investments in firms in two developing countries: Bangladesh and Malaysia. We estimate the marginal effect of R&D on the likelihood of a firm being innovative in each country and find that R&D affects Bangladeshi firms’ innovative behavior more than Malaysian firms. This finding is consistent with the law of diminishing marginal returns and the theory of economic convergence. The paper concludes with some policy suggestions for Bangladesh’s public sector as the country seeks to be more innovative.

Title: The role of alliance portfolio diversity for corporate decarbonization, circular economy and eco-innovation
Authors: Flavia Cicerelli, Alessandra Colombelli, Eva Niesten, Chiara Ravetti
Abstract: Abstract Amid growing societal and regulatory pressure to demonstrate environmental responsibility, firms are increasingly engaging in environmental alliances to address complex sustainability challenges. However, the implications of having a diverse portfolio of green alliances for a business’ progress toward environmental goals remains insufficiently understood and long-term empirical evidence on this relationship is still scant. This study adopts a novel resource-based and knowledge-based perspective to examine how environmental alliance portfolio diversity—across technological, industrial, and functional dimensions—shapes corporate environmental performance. Using data from 280 multinational companies and 1,539 environmental alliances spanning 2002–2023, our analysis reveals that all three dimensions of diversity are positively associated with overall corporate environmental performance, emission reductions, more efficient resource use, and green innovation within firms. These findings underscore the strategic importance of alliance portfolio diversity in advancing sustainability, decarbonization, and circularity goals and provide actionable insights for firms seeking to enhance specific non-financial performance metrics.

Title: Mapping entrepreneurial mobility: a machine learning perspective on firm survival and ecosystem dynamics
Authors: Angélica Pigola, Bruno Fischer, David B. Audretsch, Gustavo Hermínio Salati Marcondes de Moraes
Abstract: This study examines how entrepreneurial mobility across territorial boundaries affects firm survival within Entrepreneurial ecosystems, emphasizing the moderating role of technological intensity and ecosystem structure. Using firm-level data (2015–2020) from the PIPE/FAPESP entrepreneurship program in São Paulo, Brazil, we apply machine learning models to identify the main predictors of firm survival. The analysis reveals that mobility significantly enhances survival, particularly in medium- and high-technology industries where geographic positioning and institutional support are critical. Ecosystem attributes—such as institutional coherence, knowledge density, and market demand—emerge as key enablers of sustained performance, increasingly outweighing internal firm characteristics over time. These findings suggest that mobility operates as a systemic mechanism of knowledge circulation and adaptation, strengthening firm-level competitiveness. By integrating micro-level entrepreneurial behavior with meso-level spatial and institutional structures, the study contributes to literature by offering a data-driven understanding of how mobility shapes the spatial patterns of entrepreneurship. Policy implications highlight the importance of fostering interconnected and technologically diversified ecosystems to sustain innovation-driven ventures.

Title: Fostering regional entrepreneurial ecosystem development: the role of science and technology park networks
Authors: Andrea Ancona, Giuseppe Ceci
Abstract: Abstract Science and Technology Parks (STPs) are recognized as key drivers of regional development, although their relationship with regional entrepreneurial ecosystems (EEs) remains underexplored, particularly in terms of longitudinal and comparative analyses. This study addresses these gaps by examining how participation in a global STP network impacts regional EE development. Using a longitudinal dataset on STPs’ entry and exit dynamics in the International Association of Science and Technology Parks and Areas of Innovation (IASP) across multiple European regions, we analyze the effects of joining a global STP network on key EE dimensions. To do so, we apply a non-parametric generalization of the difference-in-differences estimator for time-series cross-sectional data. The results reveal that joining IASP strengthens the intermediary dimension of regional EEs where parks are located, facilitating talent attraction and enhancing cross-regional knowledge spillovers. These effects are both immediate and context-dependent, with more pronounced impacts observed in regions with lower GDP per capita and outside the European Union. Theoretically, the study advances the STP literature by adopting a dynamic, macro-regional perspective, extending micro-level findings and linking STPs’ increased R&D efficiency to international collaboration. Additionally, it bridges STP and EE literatures, emphasizing the role of STPs as catalysts of regional EE development. Practically, our findings provide insights for policymakers and STP managers, highlighting the importance of supporting not only the creation of STPs but also their participation in global networks to foster innovation, especially in regions with fragmented or underdeveloped policy frameworks.

Title: Competing business models in international higher education: a transatlantic comparison
Authors: David B. Audretsch, Alice Civera, Stefano Paleari, Michele Meoli
Abstract: Abstract International higher education is being reorganized by competition between business models rather than by competition between national systems alone. This Brief argues that the long-standing U.S. advantage in attracting international students and scientific talent is increasingly challenged as its premium price becomes harder to justify relative to perceived educational and career returns and growing external policy risks. The problem is not that U.S. universities have ceased to be excellent, especially at the elite end of the system. Rather, their global position has become increasingly exposed to tuition inflation, dependence on high-fee international enrollments, and political uncertainty around visas, campus conflict, and the treatment of foreign students. Europe has become a credible alternative because it offers a different value proposition: lower fees, broadly distributed quality, standardized degree structures, English-taught programs, and an explicit internationalization strategy, particularly in business schools. Yet Europe is not a new hegemon; it lacks the same concentration of global flagship universities and faces its own political and demographic constraints. The transatlantic comparison therefore points to a more plural and segmented market for global talent. For technology transfer and innovation systems, the central implication is that the geography of knowledge production will depend increasingly on how higher education systems balance cost, quality, openness, and political predictability.

Title: Intertemporal triangular spatiality of agglomeration-clustering-knowledge spillovers
Authors: Gustavo Barboza, Alessandro Braga, Aubin Duchier, Valerien Pede
Abstract: Abstract This study develops and tests an Intertemporal Triangular Spatiality (ITS) framework to explain how agglomeration, clustering, and knowledge spillovers shape firm entry and location choice in emerging markets. Using Costa Rica’s Free Trade Zone regime as a policy-discontinuity setting, the paper analyzes geocoded firm-level data for 652 firms from 1990 to 2022, distinguishing multinational enterprises and specialized exporting companies across industrial parks. The empirical strategy combines lagged Herfindahl–Hirschman concentration measures with time-varying gravity ratios capturing spatial proximity and evolving inter-park relationships, estimated through negative binomial models of new firm formation. Results show that firm entry is driven less by FTZ designation alone than by spatially embedded market structure. Immediate proximity and broader regional accessibility increase entry, while intermediate proximity generates competitive substitution. Once gravity controls are introduced, local industrial concentration discourages entry, indicating that firms seek accessible markets while avoiding excessive competition. The study contributes by formalizing ITS as a dynamic mechanism linking policy-induced FDI, technology transfer, knowledge spillovers, and entrepreneurial development. The study’s originality lies in modeling knowledge spillovers as time-dependent, spatially nested, and scale-sensitive forces shaping agglomeration and clustering outcomes.

Title: Human capital profile similarity as a sorting mechanism in mergers and acquisitions
Authors: Corrado Botta, Rachele Anconetani, Leonardo Etro, Matteo Vizzaccaro
Abstract: Abstract Mergers and acquisitions transfer technology and the knowledge embodied in a target’s workforce, and in science-based settings often complete a transfer begun in a university or research organisation. While the role of acquisitions in accessing external knowledge is well documented, less is known about whether a target’s human-capital profile shapes which firms an acquirer pairs with, even though post-acquisition productivity depends on how well the two workforces align. Drawing on absorptive-capacity theory, we treat the similarity between an acquirer’s and a target’s human-capital profile, measured the year before the deal, as a proxy for the acquirer’s capacity to absorb the target’s knowledge. We build a firm-year panel of human-capital indicators from PitchBook and compare 188,716 realised merger and acquisition pairs, announced between 2006 and 2025, against plausible alternative targets. We find that acquirers systematically select targets whose human-capital profile resembles their own, with sorting positive across seven human-capital dimensions and strongest for education. The effect weakens across national borders and strengthens across industry boundaries, consistent with similarity reducing integration frictions in more complex deals. Merging to patent records, pre-deal human-capital similarity is positively associated with post-deal patent growth, though the association is weaker among acquirers that already patent. The findings show how human capital shapes the market for corporate control and offer practical guidance for screening acquisition targets, while noting that the same similarity that eases knowledge transfer also marks the workforces most exposed to post-deal redundancy.

Title: Designing E-Services for Improving Crisis Communication in Local Municipalities: Cooperation with Apartment Associations
Authors: Jaanus Riibe, Jamal Mohamed Hassan, Rahul Sharma, Silvia Lips, Dirk Draheim
Abstract: In this study, we develop and formatively evaluate a conceptual e-service framework to support municipalities and apartment associations in crisis preparedness. Using an exploratory design-oriented case study informed by selected Action Design Research principles, we combine a World-Café-style session with older residents, expert consultations, and secondary-data analysis. The study develops the Coordination Framework for Municipal-Apartment Association Crisis Preparedness (C-MAACP Framework), which integrates municipal coordination, apartment-association participation, register-supported information management, privacy-aware access, preparedness-status visualization, and multi-channel communication. The concept was formatively evaluated with experts from the Estonian Rescue Services Agency and the Tallinn Municipal Police Department. The findings suggest that the framework can support municipal crisis preparedness by improving information coordination, clarifying stakeholder roles, and structuring cooperation between municipalities and apartment associations. The study contributes a transferable conceptual design framework while identifying implementation, adoption, legal, and privacy issues for future research.

Title: Toward Effective eHealth Communication for Efficient Utilization of Healthcare Resources: A Social Interaction and Information Needs Perspective
Authors: Yuchen Wang, Gayle Prybutok, Adeela Gulzari, Xianghui Peng, Victor Prybutok, Yajun Lu, Feng Cheng
Abstract: People’s attitudes toward online healthcare (eHealth) exhibit a spectrum of acceptance, concerns, and expectations. The low usage of people and the high adoption rate of health institutions raise colossal concerns. Bridging the evolving gap of eHealth-seeking behavior from literature and industrial practices, this research rigorously analyzes the relationships among eHealth information systems and users’ perceptions of eHealth tools with a proposed theoretical model, the eHealth-Health Belief Model-Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology2 (EHBTAUT). The article uses two rounds of primary questionnaire data from young adults aged 18–30, yielding 1,432 valid responses, to examine how health information orientation, online health behavior, eHealth literacy, social interaction needs, internet self-efficacy, and internet/social media use shape eHealth behavioral intention and utilization within EHBTAUT. The model is tested using a partial least squares structural equation modeling–probabilistic neural network (PLS–PNN) approach, supplemented by Monte Carlo simulation to assess robustness. To validate the results, this research provides an application-oriented demonstration by translating the empirically supported mechanisms into an iOS-based eHealth application and evaluating its practical relevance with 90 young adult participants. The research reveals that eHealth information-seeking motivations and internet information exchange constructs significantly affect healthcare information design, ensuring that healthcare platforms are functional and aligned with the expectations and needs of their target audience.

Title: Artificial Intelligence and the Empowerment of Vulnerable and Minority Employees: A Systematic Review
Authors: Post Raj Pokharel
Abstract: Abstract Leveraging vulnerable and minority employees poses persistent challenges, underscoring the importance of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace, which is reshaping how employees are recruited and empowered. AI appropriation processes and the pursuit of efficiency raise profound concerns about equity and employee well-being. To provide a foundation for future research, this study systematically reviews the emerging literature on AI and its impact on vulnerable and minority employees, employing a combined bibliometric analysis, principal component analysis (PCA), and thematic synthesis. This analysis of the extant body of work reveals five overarching themes: (1) AI adoption and workforce transformation, (2) bias, equity, and fairness in AI systems, (3) employee well-being, inclusion, and empowerment, (4) ethical, legal, and governance considerations, and (5) methodological approaches and tools. Across these streams, this study highlights how theoretical perspectives, ranging from congruity theory and social role theory to feminist design thinking, the diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) framework, and Procedural Justice, have been applied to interpret AI’s organisational consequences. At the same time, empirical contributions remain fragmented and uneven. This review contributes to the literature by systematically mapping how AI intersects with the experiences of marginalised employees, identifying both the risks of algorithmic exclusion and the opportunities for designing more equitable work practices. Specifically, this review contributes to the information systems literature by synthesising how AI-enabled decision systems influence equity, inclusion, and empowerment outcomes for vulnerable and minority employees. By integrating insights from organisational studies, AI ethics, and digital workplace research, the study provides a structured framework explaining how algorithmic decision systems interact with organisational governance and workforce practices.

Title: Artificial intelligence anxiety among creative professionals: Evidence from the Brazilian creative economy
Authors: Marco Aurelio de Souza Rodrigues, Veranise Jacubowski Correia Dubeux
Abstract: This study examines the dimensional structure of Artificial Intelligence Anxiety among Brazilian creative professionals through a cross-cultural adaptation and validation of the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS). While the original four-factor structure of the scale—Learning, Job Replacement, AI Configuration, and Sociotechnical Blindness—is broadly replicated, findings from EFA and CFA revealed recurring patterns of greater empirical overlap between factors, lower compartmentalization among anxiety dimensions, and atypical psychometric behavior in specific items when compared to the original validation study. Furthermore, subgroup analyses demonstrate that learning-related anxiety is higher among younger professionals, suggesting that support needs may vary across career stages. These findings are consistent with the proposition that creative workers experience AI anxiety differently from the general-population samples originally used to validate the AIAS. Theoretically, these results extend the AIAS literature to a professional population whose identity is closely tied to authorship and originality, yet whose AI-related anxiety remains empirically understudied. Practically, the findings suggest that managerial responses centered exclusively on technical upskilling may be insufficient to address concerns — such as those tied to human-machine similarity and occupational replacement — that appear to co-occur among creative professionals.

Title: Shake It Off or Take It On? Investigating the Perception of Stakeholder Demands and Cognitive Framing in Biodiversity‐Oriented Business Model Innovation
Authors: Laura Hartung‐Geyer, Patrick Spieth
Affiliations: Chair of Technology, Innovation Management and Entrepreneurship University of Kassel Kassel Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT Organizations are increasingly expected to integrate biodiversity considerations into their value logic. Little is known about the cognitive mechanisms that shape whether managers translate biodiversity‐related stakeholder expectations into intentions to pursue biodiversity‐oriented business model innovation (BMI). Drawing on cognitive framing theory, this study investigates how managers in the construction sector perceive external biodiversity stimuli and translate them into BMI intentions, focusing on opportunity and threat framing as mediating layers. Based on survey data from 137 decision‐makers in German construction firms, our study develops and empirically tests a model linking stakeholder stimuli to innovation intent, conceptualized by the Stimulus‐Organism‐Response framework. To further uncover the interpretive mechanisms, we rely on a qualitative dataset comprising 15 interviews conducted in a construction firm, thereby adopting a mixed‐method approach. Structural equation modeling shows that the perception of stakeholder stimuli affects BMI intentions indirectly through framing processes. Opportunity framing strengthens innovation intent, whereas threat framing suppresses it, though both act as mediators. The study contributes especially to the microfoundations of biodiversity‐oriented BMI by demonstrating that strategic responses arise not directly from external pressures but from managers' individual ways to interpret them cognitively. It offers practical guidance for opportunity‐oriented framing in biodiversity innovation.

Title: The costs of fiscal volatility: Evidence from firm-level data in developing countries
Authors: Rayangnewende Frans Sawadogo, Jean-Louis Combes, Pegdewende Nestor Sawadogo

Abstract: Abstract A large body of macroeconomic evidence suggests that volatility is detrimental to eco-nomic growth, yet micro-level evidence remains scarce, particularly for volatility stemming from fiscal policy. This paper examines the growth implications of fiscal volatility at the firm level. Combining country-level measures of discretionary fiscal volatility with harmonized firm-level data from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys for 58,400 firms across 74 developing countries from 2008 to 2020, we provide robust evidence that fiscal volatility significantly reduces firm sales growth. The results reveal substantial heterogeneity: medium and large firms are more resilient, while there is no mitigating effect for small firms. State-owned firms and exporters experience sharper declines. Mechanism analysis points to both demand- and supply-side channels. These findings point to the importance of predictable and well-anchored fiscal policy frameworks for supporting private sector growth in developing economies.

Title: From Sarcasm to Consumer Insight: Leveraging mT5-LSTM for Analyzing Punjabi Social Media Behavior
Authors: Jasleen Kaur, Amarjit Gill
Abstract: Sarcasm, an apparent contradiction between the literal meaning of words and their intended significance, is challenging to detect in text-based communication due to the lack of non-verbal clues. Accurate sarcasm detection enhances consumer sentiment analysis by reducing misinterpretations and providing reliable insights. The current study seeks to enhance the literature by exploring and addressing the underexplored area of sarcasm detection in Punjabi and introduces a novel hybrid model, Hybrid mT5-LSTM. This study collected 5,427 instances of Punjabi text, termed the ‘PunjSarc’ dataset, from blogs, news websites, and social media platforms and labelled as sarcastic or non-sarcastic. Moreover, the present study employed a back-translation-based augmentation strategy to address class imbalance, expanding the dataset to 5,775 instances. Besides, this study extracted textual features using the bag-of-words model with term frequency (TF) and term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) weighting schemes, as well as word embeddings. The current study conducted four experiments using textual features: baseline machine learning models, ensemble learning models, deep learning models, and the proposed hybrid model and investigated the effect of augmentation on model performance. Results show that augmentation has a mixed impact on model performance, yielding a marginal improvement in deep learning models (LSTM and Bi-LSTM) and a slight performance degradation in machine learning models (DT) and the proposed hybrid model. In addition, the experimental findings indicate that the Hybrid mT5-LSTM model, without an augmented dataset, achieves 94.29% accuracy and outperforms existing benchmark models for sarcasm detection in Punjabi text. The current study validates the efficacy of the proposed hybrid model using a statistical t-test. In addition, business owners may find accurate sarcasm detection beneficial in uncovering hidden customer dissatisfaction and offering tailored recommendations to enhance customer satisfaction and loyalty. Finally, the findings also lay the groundwork for further academic research in sarcasm detection.

Title: Mapping urban-industrial symbiosis through a business ecosystem lens
Authors: David Tianxin Shang, Yi Sun, Yongjiang Shi
Abstract: This paper examines the evolution of urban industrial symbiosis (UIS) through a business ecosystem lens. UIS, defined as the synergistic integration of urban and industrial systems where waste and by-products are repurposed as industrial inputs, has demonstrated strong potential to address climate change, urbanization challenges, and supply chain vulnerabilities. Existing UIS research has primarily focused on material flows, network structures, and policy arrangements. However, limited attention has been paid to how coordination mechanisms evolve as ecosystem interdependence and complexity increase over time. This omission is consequential because even powerful coordinators face structural limits when coordinating expanding interdependencies among heterogeneous actors and resource flows, creating a coordination gap. Drawing on case studies of Ulsan (South Korea), Händelö (Sweden), EcoPark (Hong Kong), Metro Vancouver (Canada), Kalundborg (Denmark), HS Orka (Iceland), and Kawasaki (Japan), the paper develops a process model of UIS ecosystem coordination that links generation-processing-auxiliary (G-P-A) subsystems, coordination tensions and mechanisms, and governance pathways across three analytical phases. The study advances UIS research by shifting from exchange-oriented perspectives toward dynamic ecosystem coordination and theorizing how coordination mechanisms evolve under increasing ecosystem complexity. It further extends business ecosystem theory by explaining how increasingly distributed coordination capacity sustains ecosystem resilience as growing interdependence strains centralized orchestration.

Title: Human-Centric Auditing of AI-Powered Generative Search: When Citations Diverge from Rankings
Authors: Chiang-Yu Cheng
Abstract: Generative search is reshaping digital information access by shifting users from ranked retrieval to answer-first exposure. In this environment, citations serve not only as transparency cues but also as mechanisms of source visibility allocation. To examine whether AI-generated citations align with contemporaneous search rankings, this study introduces Citation–Ranking Divergence (CRD) as a diagnostic construct for auditing epistemic misalignment in AI-powered search. We conduct a large-scale multilingual two-wave audit of Google AI Overviews using 1,500 base queries collected in Time 1 and re-collected in Time 2, yielding 3,000 wave-specific observations across five language–region locales before eligibility filtering. The results show incomplete but structured alignment between generative citations and SERP rankings. Counterintuitively, citations are neither fully detached from rankings nor simply reflective of them; instead, they remain partially anchored to ranked visibility while selectively re-concentrating exposure through a narrower subset of sources. We further identify a typology of divergence patterns, showing that visibility reallocation follows recurring forms rather than a single uniform logic. Cross-wave analyses indicate that these core patterns are reasonably stable. This study develops CRD as a scalable auditing framework, reconceptualizes citations as a visibility-allocation mechanism, and advances research on platform accountability, algorithmic transparency, and knowledge visibility governance.

Title: What rates of return do firms expect from innovation investments?
Authors: Huan Yang, Marc Cowling, Syahirah Abdul Rahman, Tim Vorley
Abstract: Abstract Innovation investments are risky and uncertain in their outcomes. Thus, innovating firms should expect higher rates of return if their investments are successful to compensate for the additional risk and uncertainty. Further, financiers also have different appetites for risk and uncertainty thus they will only fund projects that fit their risk-return profile. In this paper we use a large UK firm investment and finance decision making survey to establish what rates of return firms expect from their innovation investments and whether this differs across different types of investment financiers. Our core results show that process and product/service innovation investments have an expected return of 15 to 20% and IT investments an expected return of 10 to 15%. This implies that IT investments are perceived to be less risky than other innovation investments, therefore with relatively lower expected returns. From our econometric analysis, it is also the case that firms that finance innovation investments with retained cash have lower expected returns whilst firms attracting external equity have the highest expected returns. Our findings add to our understanding of what firms expect when they invest in innovation and how this is shaped by the type of finance they use.

Title: Will your AI turn backers away? Evidence from Kickstarter's AI-use disclosure policy
Authors: Sonika Singhal, Yeongin Kim, Seonjun Kang, Victoria Yoon
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how creative work is produced, raising new questions about authenticity, originality, and human effort in entrepreneurial settings. We examine how platform-mandated AI-use disclosure is associated with crowdfunding outcomes, using Kickstarter’s 2023 disclosure policy and a dataset of over 63,000 campaigns launched between 2022 and 2024. Drawing on signaling theory, we argue that an AI-use label functions as a platform-governed cue that backers may interpret as signaling reduced human effort, potentially shaping how they evaluate creators and campaigns. Empirically, we find that AI-use disclosure is associated with a significantly lower likelihood of campaign success, with this negative association concentrated in reduced backer participation. The disclosure penalty is weaker when campaign descriptions are more subjective and easier to read, but stronger in technology-oriented campaigns where human expertise and originality are especially salient. It is also weaker for creators with stronger prior track records. Our findings identify AI-use disclosure as a novel platform-governed signal in crowdfunding, contribute to research on how platform-designed information environments shape user evaluations, and highlight potential unintended consequences of AI transparency requirements for platform design and policy.

Title: Does AI erode street-level discretion? A mixed-methods study on automated decision-making in China's tax authorities
Authors: Jingjing Li, Chuanshen Qin, Lan Xue
Abstract: In the context of the increasing adoption of AI-based automated decision-making in the public sector, this paper explores the complex relationship between AI automation and street-level discretion. Existing research has produced mixed findings on whether AI curtails or enables discretion, but has paid less attention to regulation-oriented street-level bureaucratic settings and to how algorithm literacy conditions officials' perceived discretion. This paper employs a mixed-methods approach to examine how discretion-as-perceived unfolds under AI automation in the regulation-oriented street-level bureaucrats, i.e., tax authorities in China, combining a survey experiment ( n = 310) and in-depth interviews with frontline tax officials. Our quantitative results provides support for the AI's enabling effect by revealing that AI automation is associated with higher street-level bureaucrats' discretion perception. The mechanisms are further elucidated by the qualitative findings that AI expands street-level bureaucrats' action resources through judgment improvement and decision-making legitimization, with human autonomy of the tax street-level bureaucrats maintained. Furthermore, we imply that the street-level bureaucrats' discretion-as-perceived is shaped by their algorithm literacy, as both quantitative and qualitative findings indicate that knowledge of algorithms (KOA) negatively moderates the relationship between AI and discretion-as-perceived, whereas reflection on algorithms (ROA) has the opposite moderation effect. This study contributes to the discretion debate under the AI digitalization age by providing a systematic investigation with theoretical and practical implications discussed.

Title: A Hybrid Simulation Modelling Framework for Stress Testing Rare Earth Element-Centric Semiconductor Supply Chains
Authors: Naoum Tsolakis, Wei Nie, Zhong Guan, Yongxu Zhao, Fangrui Li, Mariel Alem Fonseca, Deepesh Jayasekara, Garry Clawson, Gavin Harper, Mukesh Kumar
Affiliations: University of Cambridge; University of Birmingham, Edgbaston
Abstract: Semiconductor supply chains (SCs) depend on geographically concentrated rare earth element inputs and face systemic risks from geopolitical disruption, policy intervention, and capacity constraints across multiple decision-making layers. Existing stress testing approaches often quantify fulfilment loss without attributing it to strategic capacity shortages, tactical sourcing-access constraints, or operational congestion, even though each requires a different intervention. This study develops a hybrid simulation modelling framework integrating System Dynamics (SD), Agent-Based Modelling (ABM), and Discrete Event Simulation (DES) as necessary analytical approaches per decision-making layer: SD captures long-term capacity stocks and policy feedback (macro-level); ABM captures heterogeneous monthly sourcing and inventory decisions (meso-level); and DES captures stochastic weekly fabrication and shipment execution (micro-level). Applied to India’s cerium-centric semiconductor SC through 247 experiments, 12,350 simulation runs and an additional 1,400 runs of sensitivity analysis, the analysis shows that upstream cerium capacity disruptions are largely buffered, whereas loss of qualified fabrication capacity causes severe fulfilment collapse. Stable DES cycle times further confirm that this failure arises from sourcing access rather than operational congestion. This cross-layer diagnostic signal is only detectable when all three modelling layers are present. Managerially, the hybrid simulation modelling framework reframes stress testing as a multi-level tool that identifies not only whether an SC fails, but also where failure emerges and which intervention is appropriate.

Title: The mission trap: government dependence and two paths of technology commercialization in aerospace and defense ventures
Authors: KwangWook Gang, Boreum Choi
Abstract: Public funding is widely used to accelerate technology commercialization, yet its effects on venture outcomes remain contested. Building on dual legitimacy theory, we propose a two-path framework in which government-program commercialization — attainment of a Phase II award under the U.S. Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program, the milestone at which a venture advances government-funded prototype development toward commercialization — and market commercialization (initial public offering or acquisition) function as distinct forms of legitimacy granted by different audiences. Using a sample of aerospace and defense ventures (1115 firms; U.S. primary sample of 652; 2010–2024), we find that financing-round frequency exhibits a robust inverted-U relationship with market commercialization, and that government funding dependence — the Non-Diluted Financing Ratio (NDFR), the share of capital from non-dilutive government sources — raises government-program commercialization but shows no significant association with market commercialization. Ventures combining intensive financing rounds with high government dependence form a Mission Trap: they attain government-program commercialization at the highest rates yet rarely convert it into market exits. Timing analyses are consistent with a maturation component and a possible configurational component, though censoring limits inference. These findings reframe the public funding paradox as a path-selection phenomenon, with implications for innovation policy and venture financing in procurement-dependent sectors.
