Title: Different strokes for different folks? Cross-disciplinary syntheses and directions on growth
Authors: Ludvig Levasseur, David Audretsch, Siri Terjesen, Shibin Thali Parambil
Abstract: Firm growth and scaling are inherently multi-dimensional, time-sensitive, and complex phenomena. Yet, the scholarship investigating them overwhelmingly relies on either quantitative or qualitative methods in isolation. We argue that this methodological singularity produces a fragmented and incomplete understanding, and that mixed methods research offers a more powerful lens for capturing the processual, contextual, and dynamic character of growth and scaling. In this paper, we provide a first cross-disciplinary narrative synthesis of the personal, firm-level, and contextual determinants of firm growth and a second synthesis of the relationship between entrepreneurship and economic growth. Drawing on these syntheses, we develop an illustrative cross-disciplinary and mixed methods agenda on the digital entrepreneurship–growth and scaling relationship, highlighting how the porous boundaries and distributed agency characteristic of digital entrepreneurship call for longitudinal, policy-sensitive research designs that combine both statistical and narrative inquiry. Taking an ‘applied’ perspective, we also focus on two sequential designs and provide examples. Across our illustrations, we show how mixed methods can generate insights into the how , how much , how fast , and why of growth and scaling that neither method alone can produce. We conclude with recommendations for scholars navigating the conceptual and measurement challenges of this research domain and a call for more interdisciplinary, processual, and methodologically pluralistic investigation.

Title: Neither community nor corporation? A deeper look at decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs)
Authors: Ying-Ying Hsieh, Phanish Puranam, Noam Gelman-Hofstadter
Affiliations: Imperial Business School, Management and Entrepreneurship Department, Imperial College London, South Kensington Campus, London, SW7 2AZ, United Kingdom. email: y.hsieh@imperial.ac.uk; INSEAD, 1, Ayer Rajah Avenue , 138676 Singapore. email: phanish.puranam@insead.edu; DeepDAO Ventures Ltd., Rothschild Boulevard 22 , Tel-Aviv, 6688218 Israel. email: noam.hof.gel@gmail.com; Public Advocacy Department , Public Committee Against Torture in
Abstract: Abstract The surge in decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) since 2018 arguably represents the “great decentralization experiment” of our times. Traditionally, firms align actors through financial incentives and centralized authority; communities motivate through shared values and self-selection. DAOs, in their ideal form, promise to combine the scalability of the former with the participation of the latter. A growing body of research on individual DAOs, however, casts doubt on whether this promise is fulfilled. What do DAOs’ departures from their design aspirations reveal about decentralization, autonomy, and organization itself? We study this question using DeepDAO, the largest systematic dataset on DAOs to date. Our findings confirm that most DAOs are not meaningfully decentralized, autonomous, or coherently organizational. Studying these departures from design aspirations yields three theoretical recalibrations. First, decentralization operates differently at different levels: The DAO ecosystem is decentralized, but individual DAOs are not. Decision-making power in DAOs is concentrated through asymmetries in token ownership and chronically low participation. Second, autonomy is polysemous in ways that the DAO experiment lays bare: the term conflates automation with independence, and most DAOs achieve neither. Third, low participation rates and de facto concentration of decision-making rights reframe the question of what it means to be an organization at all, not as a binary condition but as a profile of degrees across multiple dimensions. DAOs thus force a re-specification of concepts that organization science has long treated as settled and illuminate the limits of technology as a decentralizing force.

Title: Using leverage points to identify interventions for transitioning the Dutch road infrastructure sector toward sustainability
Authors: Angie Ruiz, André Nijhof, Maurits Sanders, Fredy Ivar Sierra-Fernández, Joanne Vinke-de Kruijf
Abstract: The transition toward sustainability in infrastructure sectors requires interventions that address systemic lock-ins rather than isolated technological improvements. However, innovation ecosystem research offers only limited guidance on how public-sector-driven ecosystems can be intentionally steered toward sustainability under conditions of structural inertia. This study employs Donella Meadows’ leverage points framework to identify and categorize potential systemic interventions in the Dutch road infrastructure innovation ecosystem. Using an action-oriented research design conducted over 1.5 years with public clients, contractors, and knowledge institutions, the study identifies 25 interventions across five thematic areas. The findings show that interventions predominantly target system design and feedback structures, the strengthening of governance, foresight, and integration capabilities rather than focusing on parameter-level change. This highlights how transformations in public-sector innovation ecosystems emerge through the gradual reconfiguration of rules, information flows, and coordination mechanisms. The study contributes to innovation ecosystem research by demonstrating how leverage points can be used to guide and structure ecosystem-level intervention strategies and support deliberate steering of public-sector-driven innovation ecosystems toward sustainability.

TIS subsystems and modes of innovation: the case of hydrogen-powered aviation
Authors: Lennart Gruen, Richard Hanke-Rauschenbach, Julian Hoelzen, Ingo Liefner, Sebastian Losacker
Affiliations: Leibniz University Hannover; Stellenbosch University; Justus Liebig University Giessen; Lund University
Abstract: Recent technological advancements in hydrogen-powered aviation are significantly influenced by start-up companies, despite substantial market entry barriers. To investigate the role of these emerging actors in the sustainability transition of the aviation sector, we compare the innovation activities of established and emerging hydrogen-powered aircraft manufacturers through qualitative expert interviews. Our findings reveal distinct differences in the innovation modes of these two groups: established manufacturers pursue a ‘breakthrough’ innovation mode, while emerging manufacturers adopt a ‘bricolage’ innovation mode. Additionally, these groups contribute differently to the Technological Innovation System (TIS) functionality. We argue that each group forms a distinct TIS subsystem due to substantial institutional differences that uniquely impact the TIS. Consequently, we identify multi-(sub)system dynamics as a critical factor for the future development of the hydrogen-powered aviation TIS.

Title: On sci-tech paradigms: an essay on the economics of innovation
Authors: Nicola De Liso
Affiliations: Department of Law – Economics Division, University of Salento , Via per Monteroni snc 73100 Lecce , . email: nicola.deliso@unisalento.it
Abstract: Abstract Scholars working in the evolutionary economics of innovation are familiar with the concept of the technological paradigm and, indirectly, with that of the scientific paradigm. The former derives from the latter, and was developed in recognition of the relative autonomy of technology from science. In this work, I reconsider the relationship between science and technology, arguing that, in a few important cases, technology can no longer be meaningfully distinguished from science. In such cases, science and technology converge to form a sci-tech agglomerate, hence the notion of a sci-tech paradigm. The fundamental role played by economic incentives in promoting this convergence is taken into account. Acceptance of this notion implies the need to revise policy frameworks that rely on indicators calibrated for conditions that no longer exist.

Title: Editorial Board
When does generative AI adoption pay off? ethical governance as a dynamic capability in SMEs
Authors: Tahereh Hasani
Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) offers substantial innovation opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), yet its performance benefits vary considerably across firms. Drawing on the resource-based view (RBV) and dynamic capabilities perspective, this study theorizes ethical AI governance as a capability bundle—comprising transparency/explainability (TE), fairness/bias control (FB), privacy/data protection (PD), and accountability/responsibility (ACCT)—that conditions the innovation payoff from GenAI adoption. Using 218 usable manager responses from Canadian SMEs, we test the proposed model using covariance-based structural equation modeling in AMOS 22 and examine moderation through multigroup analysis with measurement-invariance checks. The results show that GenAI adoption is positively associated with innovation performance, while TE, PD, and ACCT significantly strengthen this relationship. In contrast, FB exhibits a significant negative moderating effect, a pattern consistent with a short-run maturity-stage trade-off in which overly rigid or poorly integrated fairness controls may slow early experimentation in resource-constrained SMEs, even though fairness assurance remains essential for responsible scaling. The findings also reveal asymmetric adoption drivers: green-innovation orientation is the strongest positive driver, whereas carbon-footprint pressure and economic disruption are negatively associated with adoption. Higher innovation performance, in turn, is positively associated with adaptability and resilience, operational efficiency, and revenue growth. Overall, the study reframes ethical AI governance from compliance overhead to a dynamic capability and identifies governance-related boundary conditions that help explain when GenAI adoption is associated with stronger innovation performance and downstream firm outcomes in SMEs.

Title: From Explainability to Actionability: a Tiered Adaptable Multi-Agent Framework with Agent Reasoning Tools for Collaborative Failure Recovery
Authors: Jie Tao, Lina Zhou
Abstract: Abstract Effective human-AI collaboration, especially in failure scenarios, requires systems that function as active partners rather than static tools. This research addresses this requirement by introducing a tiered multi-agent architecture grounded in Human-Centered eXplainable AI principles. The architecture consists of three novel design artifacts: tiered reasoning that adapts explanation depth to failure severity, a traceable memory bus for auditability, and flexible reasoning tools for enhanced adaptability. These designs enable agents to not only perform evidence-based diagnoses of performance gaps but devise recovery strategies and propose actionable improvement plans as well. We empirically evaluate this architecture on an aspect term extraction task using hybrid methods that combine performance comparisons against state-of-the-art baselines, human expert user studies, and multi-role user simulations. The results demonstrate that our architecture significantly enhances both task performance and failure recovery diagnosis and plans. We then validate the generalizability of our architecture with a second task of comparable complexity. This research contributes an adaptable and generalizable framework and foundational artifacts for trustworthy AI teammates.

Title: Configuring hybrid agency: How both technological agency and human agency drive blockchain-based risk mitigation
Authors: Yongjun Wei, Steven Si, Yongyi Shou
Abstract: The latest research indicates that blockchain technology (BCT) is a powerful tool for organizational risk management, but enterprises often struggle to fully utilize its potential and effectiveness in practical operations. This study explores the configuration of BCT agency mechanism and human agent mechanism in the idiosyncratic risk mitigation that drives success and failure. By leveraging the hybrid agency theory and employing crisp-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (csQCA) on a sample of Chinese listed firms, we identify distinct pathways to risk mitigation success and failure. The findings of this study reveal that successful risk mitigation is not solely dependent on maximizing technical features or application scope; it often depends on strategically limiting the application scope of the technology to match the organization's governance capabilities. On the contrary, failure typically occurs when enterprises over-expand their technology deployment without the necessary internal expertise or platform dominance to manage this expansion. This study challenges technological determinism and emphasizes the necessity of hierarchical control in blockchain governance. Moreover, by shifting the research focus from structured task allocation to configurational coordination of governance capabilities, we have advanced the hybrid agent theory. This indicates that the feasibility of agent technology depends on whether human capabilities are sufficient to coordinate the scope of the deployed technology.

Title: Investigating the effect of notification deactivation on social media app usage: A longitudinal experiment
Authors: Na Liu, Yi Wu, Yi Shen, Carol Hsu
Abstract: Given the potential effects of social media use on health and productivity, it is important to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions that encourage healthier usage patterns. Drawing on dual-system theory, this study examines whether reducing external cues, specifically through notification deactivation, can shift users from impulsive to more reflective patterns of social media engagement. In addition, we investigate how individual differences in social media impulsivity influence usage behavior in the absence of external triggers. Through a 21-day field experiment, the findings indicate that notification deactivation temporarily reduced social media usage during the treatment period but failed to sustain these effects after the intervention ended. Furthermore, individuals with higher levels of social media impulsivity, particularly those exhibiting strong positive and negative urgency, continued to spend more time on social media applications despite notification deactivation.

Title: Generative AI Labeling, Communication Style, and Perceived Emotional Support in Chatbot Interactions among International Students
Authors: Jian-Ren Hou, Maria Bellaniar Ismiati
Abstract: Chatbots are increasingly used to support emotional well-being. This study examines how formal communication style and chatbot identity label influence users’ perceptions of emotional support. We developed Airbud, a generative AI chatbot presented under different identity labels (Generative AI vs. traditional chatbot) and collected data from 450 international students using formal and informal communication styles. Using structural equation modeling, the results show that formal communication style enhances perceived tie strength, while perceived warmth strengthens its effect on social presence, perceived tie strength, and emotional relief. Interaction satisfaction shapes perceived chatbot support for loneliness, sadness, and anxiety. Perceived chatbot support refers to users’ perceived support efficacy rather than actual clinical improvement or measurable emotional change. Multi-group analysis shows that formal communication style is less strongly related to perceived judgment under the GenAI label. These findings highlight the importance of communication style, perceived warmth, and identity labels in chatbots for international students.

Title: Creative Destruction Within Platform Ecosystems: The Role of Platform Technological Capability in Generativity
Authors: Alireza Rasouli, Iman Miremadi
Affiliations: Graduate School of Management and Economics Sharif University of Technology Tehran Iran
Abstract: ABSTRACT Creative destruction, though underexamined in platform ecosystem research, is a core mechanism of innovation and economic transformation. By disrupting established structures, it enables technological progress and increases diversity among innovators. This study investigates the dynamics of complementors within platform ecosystems and their interactions with platform owners' technological capabilities, highlighting their joint influence on generativity. Drawing on data from video game platforms, patent registrations, and quantitative analyses, we integrate creative destruction and technological capability to evaluate their combined impact on innovation outcomes. The findings indicate that platform owners' technological capability strengthens the positive effect of creative destruction on generativity. Furthermore, technological capability equips platform owners with the governance tools necessary to navigate the complexities of a diverse influx of new innovators. The study advances theory by unpacking the interplay between creative destruction and technological capability in platform ecosystems and offers managerial insights for leveraging these dynamics to sustain innovation and competitive advantage.

Title: Digital transformation in the global south: Balancing risks and building resilience
Authors: Sonel Pyram, Bohdan Trembovelskyi, Tobias Mettler
Abstract: Digital transformation (DT) is increasingly recognized as vital to enhancing the organizational performance of public sector worldwide. Yet many DT projects fail to achieve their intended outcomes. We argue that these failures are partly attributable to the risk environments surrounding projects before and after implementation. Although DT literature emphasizes risk management and resilience, limited attention has been given to integrating both into DT project design. This paper addresses this gap by examining how these considerations are embedded as strategic elements in DT projects in the Global South. Using a convergent-parallel mixed-methods approach, we analyzed 32 World Bank Group DT project proposals from governments in the Global South using BERTopic-based natural language processing, triangulated with thematic analysis of 13 semi-structured interviews with third-party stakeholders. Findings reveal a systematic gap between resilience assumptions embedded in project designs and the contextual realities of implementation. Specifically, limited local capacity, governance fragmentation, remoteness, geopolitical conflict, and dependence on external suppliers can significantly affect project outputs and outcomes. We conclude by proposing project-level mechanisms to strengthen resilience and identify directions for future research on government-led DT projects in developing-country contexts.

Title: Exploratory versus exploitative innovation in central state-owned enterprises: the role of administrative rank
Authors: Haiping Fu, Hongquan Chen, Saixing Zeng, Ruochen Zeng
Abstract: State-owned enterprises (SOEs) play a pivotal role in national innovation systems, yet their dual mandate of serving public objectives while remaining commercially viable makes it difficult to balance exploratory and exploitative innovation. We examine how administrative rank, a formal position within the party-state hierarchy, shapes this balance in Chinese central SOEs. Using a multi-source panel dataset of Chinese central SOEs from 2003 to 2023 and patent-based measures of exploratory and exploitative innovation, we find that higher administrative rank is primarily associated with greater exploratory innovation, alongside a negative relationship with exploitative innovation. Absorptive capacity reinforces the exploratory orientation associated with administrative rank, whereas deep internal hierarchies attenuate it. These findings suggest that administrative rank shapes innovation portfolios by structuring access to policy-backed resources, frontier knowledge, and strategically salient incentives. By highlighting differentiation within the central SOE sector, this study extends resource-based and incentive-based views of SOE innovation and shows how politically structured organizational position helps explain the allocation of effort between exploration and exploitation.

Title: The differential impact of India’s industrial liberalization on firms’ R&D: does import competition matter?
Authors: Hariom Arora, Ruchi Sharma
Affiliations: Discipline of Economics, School of Humanities and Social Sciences, Indian Institute of Technology Indore , Khandwa Road, Simrol, Madhya Pradesh , 453552
Abstract: Abstract Market competition and production scale jointly shape firms’ innovation incentives. Industrial delicensing in India provides a quasi-natural experiment to examine the influence of market conditions on firms’ R&D. Hence, we investigate the long-term impact of industrial delicensing on firm-level R&D from 1988 to 2020 using a staggered difference-in-differences framework. We further study the heterogeneous effects of import competition in shaping the relationship between industrial delicensing and firm-level innovation. The analysis finds a positive and statistically significant impact of delicensing on firms’ R&D stock. However, the results reveal a varying response based on the degree of import competition, as firms facing high import competition increase R&D spending, whereas those in low import competition industries do not respond in a similar manner. These findings align with theoretical predictions that competitive environments stimulate innovation. The results also reveal heterogeneity in treatment effects across firm size and age.

Title: Explainable AI model for predicting customer service communication effectiveness: A computational design science approach
Authors: Xin Liu, Lin Jia, Gemin Liang, Yifan Yu
Abstract: Effective communication between customer service representatives (CSRs) and customers is essential for maintaining customer relationships and improving operational performance. Although firms have increasingly used AI technologies to evaluate customer service communication effectiveness, existing approaches primarily rely on dialogue texts while ignoring sequential communication strategies that reveal CSRs' underlying intentions. Furthermore, communication strategies are often quantified through manual coding, limiting scalability and explainability. Consequently, it remains unclear how individual strategies and their combinations contribute to AI-based predictions of communication effectiveness. Following the Computational Design Science research paradigm and Aristotle's Rhetoric Theory, this study proposes an explainable customer service communication effectiveness prediction model with text-strategy dual input based on the Transformer Encoder architecture (ExTSdiT). To enable automated strategy quantification, we design few-shot Chain-of-Thought prompts to guide large language models in annotating communication strategy labels from CSR utterances. Customized model explainability techniques are further employed to analyze the effects of individual strategies and their combinations at the dialogue-turn level. The framework is evaluated on a large-scale real-world customer service call dataset. Results show that the proposed model outperforms benchmark methods across multiple metrics and exhibits robust performance in ablation and stability analyses. The explainability results can support customer service communication quality inspection, and facilitate data-driven customer service training.

Title: Simulating the Future of Innovation: A Data-Grounded, Multi-Agent LLM Framework for R&D Collaboration Planning in Urban Mobility
Authors: Yong-Jae Lee
Abstract: Cross-domain R&D collaboration in urban mobility is stalled by disciplinary silos that existing foresight methods cannot bridge. This study proposes a multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework that converts patent-based convergence signals into actionable industry–academia R&D proposals. Using 26,399 WIPO patent applications (2000–2024), the system identifies high-potential technology pairs via Bayesian long short-term memory (LSTM) signal detection, builds expert personas from inventor records, retrieves academic collaborators through ArXiv queries, and produces structured R&D roadmaps through LangGraph-orchestrated three-phase dialogues. A Two-Track evaluation separates an upper-bound capability demonstration (Track A) from primary validity evidence (Track B), which employs six non-generative discriminative scorers to substantially reduce evaluator–generator circularity (pipeline advantage: Δ = + 0.275, d = 2.227). Expert evaluation confirms strong inter-rater reliability (intraclass correlation = 0.918, n = 24), though a calibration gap indicates automated scores are systematically higher than human ratings. Limitations include short-window signal detection, proxy-level automated scoring, and unconfirmed real-world feasibility.

Title: Emotional Resonance and Multimedia Presence: Unpacking Virality and Misinformation Risks in the Generative AI Era
Authors: Venu Bhaskar Puthineedi, Ashish Kumar Jha
Abstract: Social media platforms shape political discourse, yet their emotional and multimedia affordances also create fertile ground for misinformation. This study examines how emotional resonance and multimedia cues drive engagement and within-platform virality in Reddit’s largest political communities, offering implications for theory and governance in the Generative AI era. Using 17,548 posts and 1.5 million comments, we apply deep learning models (BERT, DistilRoBERTa) to capture fine-grained affective expressions. Results show that negative emotions—especially anger, disgust, and fear—are strongly associated with engagement and within-platform virality, while positive emotions have weaker effects. Multimedia presence significantly increases emotional intensity and reach, highlighting the importance of peripheral multimedia cues in emotional engagement and amplification. Additional associations involving moderator status and account-level authentication characteristics suggest that governance-related features may also be linked to lower emotional amplification. These findings clarify organic amplification dynamics that become especially consequential in contemporary social media environments.

Title: The designer's turn: Reconfiguring professional identity for project innovation in the generative AI era
Authors: Ming Hung Hsieh, Rong Chen, Hui Chun Lee
Abstract: The disruption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in creative industries is profound. While AI increasingly acts as a proactive partner in ideation, little is known about how this collaboration relates to professional identity reconstruction and project performance. To examine this, we focus on spatial design (architecture and interior design), where digital generation must translate into strict physical constraints and commercial reality. To understand the human foundations of AI-driven innovation, we conducted a mixed-methods study: 10 qualitative interviews (Gioia methodology) and a survey of 223 spatial design projects from Taiwan and Mainland China. Findings support a mediating role for Professional Identity Reconstruction (PIR) between perceived human-AI collaboration and perceived project performance. Specifically, we uncover a shift from the identity of traditional “craftsmen” to “strategic decision-makers.” Professionals who successfully navigate this reconstruction no longer act as mere manual executors; instead, they exercise strategic judgment over machine-generated outputs. This strategic elevation is associated with an enhanced ability to interpret, constrain, and translate raw AI variations into valuable project outcomes. This paper offers two key contributions. First, it refines the assumption of automatic technological dividends: while direct human-AI collaboration correlates with internal process efficiency, it has an indirect association with external market success through human strategic translation. Second, it advances innovation management literature by conceptualizing PIR as one plausible translating pathway. Our findings suggest that as AI automates execution, the realization of market value shifts toward strategic direction. Ultimately, we advise managers to foster workflows prioritizing human evaluative inputs, ensuring algorithmic capabilities are firmly anchored within professional boundaries and commercial realities.

Title: Resource orchestration in incubator management: Evidence from multiple cases
Authors: Xuelin Wang, Xiaofeng Qin, Yeming Gong, Ajay Kumar, Xinyuan Lu
Abstract: Incubators play a vital role in entrepreneurial ecosystems by providing start-ups with resources such as funding, mentorship, and access to networks. Incubator systems differ from traditional organizations because start-ups remain legally and strategically independent, which limits hierarchical control and makes coordination inherently relational. However, existing research tends to emphasize the effects of individual resources, paying less attention to how incubators orchestrate resources through ongoing interaction with ventures, leaving unresolved why incubators with similar resource bases often produce markedly different outcomes. Thus, drawing on Resource Orchestration Theory, this study examines how incubators structure, bundle, and leverage resources, and how orchestration operates across multiple levels to shape start-up growth and incubator performance. Based on a qualitative multi-case study, we identify a four-stage cyclical orchestration process in which incubators (1) structure a foundational resource base, (2) provide tailored initial resource packages, (3) dynamically reconfigure bundled resources as ventures evolve, and (4) activate start-up feedback. Feedback takes concrete forms such as alumni mentoring, network bridging, investment connections, and reputational endorsements, which replenish the incubator's resource base and enable subsequent rounds of support. We further theorize a multi-level mechanism comprising incubator orchestration, start-up orchestration, and joint orchestration; joint orchestration operates through coordinated resource acquisition, bundling, and leveraging, helping explain outcome heterogeneity beyond resource stock differences.

Title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee innovation: Collaboration modes, idea journey, and decline in creative psychological ownership
Authors: Ling Tan, Xin Cao, Chunlan Ou, Ya Li, Xiaojie Wu
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly used by employees to support creative idea generation, yet less is known about its psychological consequences for employees’ subsequent willingness to remain engaged with those ideas. Drawing on psychological ownership theory, we examine whether GAI usage is associated with lower creative psychological ownership (CPO)—the extent to which employees perceive creative ideas as “theirs”—and, in turn, weaker intentions to elaborate, champion, and implement those ideas. We further propose that this relationship varies across human–GAI collaboration modes, with the negative relationship between GAI usage and CPO being more pronounced under GAI-centric collaboration than under human-centric or symbiotic collaboration. Across two scenario-based experiments (Studies 1–2), two task-based studies involving actual GAI interaction (Studies 3–4), and a multi-wave field study (Study 5), the findings provide converging, although not uniform, evidence for the proposed relationships. A mini meta-analysis further indicates an overall negative association between GAI usage and CPO and positive associations between CPO and downstream innovation-related intentions. Overall, the findings identify a potential psychological cost of GAI-assisted idea generation. They also show how collaboration modes may shape employees’ perceived ownership of ideas and their intentions to continue developing and advancing them.

Title: How does digital transformation and Global Innovation Network Embedding affect ESG performance of multinational enterprises? Empirical evidence from an Eastern innovation pattern
Authors: Jintao Lu, Zuxin Song, Luu Duc Toan Huynh, Malin Song, Armando Papa
Abstract: As an important manifestation of data-driven technological innovation paradigms, digital transformation has become a key pathway through which multinational enterprises reshape their innovation processes, enhance global competitiveness, and achieve sustainable value creation. It not only transforms firms’ modes of knowledge creation, organizational coordination mechanisms, and resource allocation logic, but also creates new opportunities for multinational enterprises to deepen their global innovation network embedding and improve ESG performance. However, existing studies have rarely systematically explored the impact mechanism of digital transformation on ESG performance from the perspective of global innovation network embedding. Grounded in the resource-based theory and social network theory, using panel data of Chinese A-share listed multinational enterprises from 2010 to 2022, the impact and mechanism of digital transformation on ESG performance in multinational enterprises were empirically analyzed by employing the two-way fixed effects model, the mediation effect model and the moderation effect model. Results indicate that, (1) Digital transformation has a significantly positive effect on the ESG performance. (2) The mechanism through which digital transformation enhances ESG performance lies in accelerating the global innovation network embedding of multinational enterprises. (3) Internal control quality strengthens the positive effect of digital transformation on ESG performance, whereas external environmental uncertainty weakens this effect. (4) The digital transformation has a stronger incentive effect on ESG performance for large-scale, manufacturing, and technology and labor-intensive multinational enterprises. The obtained conclusions contribute to fully leveraging the driving effect of digital transformation by multinational enterprises in the global value chain and provide empirical evidence that such firms can enhance their global collaborative innovation capability and sustainable competitive advantage through digital transformation.

Title: PATTERN-X: Guiding sustainable innovation in intelligent lighting systems through an explainable AI framework for technology convergence forecasting
Authors: Yong-Jae Lee
Abstract: Strategic R&D management requires foresight tools that are dynamic, uncertainty-aware, and transparent, yet most existing approaches remain static, deterministic, and difficult to interpret. This study introduces PATTERN-X (Patent Analytics Through Temporal Network Evaluation and Reasoning with eXplainability), an explainable AI framework integrating temporal patent network analysis, Bayesian deep learning, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Using 4167 European Patent Office patents in the Intelligent Lighting Systems (ILS) domain (1981–2024), the framework is empirically validated within the European ILS innovation ecosystem. The study addresses three research questions: RQ1 examines how temporal network analysis can reveal the evolution of technology innovation ecosystems; RQ2 investigates how probabilistic deep learning can quantify predictive uncertainty for risk-aware R&D decision-making; and RQ3 explores how generative AI can translate quantitative forecasts into evidence-based strategic narratives. Addressing RQ1, temporal co-classification network analysis reveals ecosystem evolution from 3 to 16 technology clusters and a shift in centrality toward digital control and vehicle-integrated technologies. Addressing RQ2, a Bayesian LSTM achieves an MAE of 0.89, an 88% strategic hit rate, and well-calibrated uncertainty estimates (PICP = 0.91 against a nominal 95% interval, reflecting a slight undercoverage typical of variational approximations), enabling risk-sensitive evaluation of convergence opportunities. Addressing RQ3, a CPC-guided RAG system generates evidence-grounded strategic narratives with high faithfulness (0.85; κ = 0.82), translating probabilistic forecasts into auditable managerial explanations. Together, these results demonstrate how dynamic analysis, uncertainty quantification, and explainable generative AI can enhance technology convergence forecasting and strategic innovation management.

Title: Editorial Board
From discovery to deployment: technology transfer as a supply chain process
Authors: Benjamin Agyei-Owusu, Donald Siegel, David Waldman, Mohan Gopalakrishnan, Saurabh Mishra
Abstract: Supply chains are increasingly central to converting scientific discoveries and technological knowledge into operational, commercial, and societal value. Yet supply chain management (SCM) scholarship, like adjacent fields, has approached technology transfer (TT) as a transfer event in which value is presumed to follow once rights or knowledge change hands. We reconceptualize TT as a discovery-to-deployment supply chain process: five recursive stages (discovery, development and protection, scaling and commercialization, deployment and use, and renewal) coordinated by distributed, co-specialized capabilities. A review of 67 articles in eight core SCM journals demonstrates that the field, constrained by the transfer-event framing, has concentrated on sourcing, IP governance, licensing, and commercialization, while leaving operational assimilation, downstream deployment, use support, and feedback-based renewal underdeveloped. Reading these tendencies as the footprint of a shared assumption, we develop a research agenda around four shifts: from technology transactions to capability coordination, isolated events to longitudinal processes, upstream sourcing to network-wide deployment, and one-way transfer to feedback-based renewal. This reconceptualization integrates two literatures that have developed apart. First, we give technology transfer research a process-and-coordination lens that helps explain why some technologies scale and endure while others stall at the license or pilot stage. Second, we extend SCM’s domain from coordinating materials, products, and information to coordinating technological knowledge and capabilities.

Title: Designing humanoid agents for economic decision-making with LLMs: A framework based on cognitive architecture and dual-process theory
Authors: Liming Zhao, Haichao Zheng, Bin Zhu, Chao Liu
Abstract: Humanoid agents are intelligent entities designed to think and behave in ways that resemble human cognition and actions. Despite their growing significance in economic decision-making studies, there is a lack of comprehensive theoretical frameworks to guide the design of such agents. Powered by large language models (LLMs), this paper addresses this gap by proposing a framework that integrates cognitive architecture and dual-process theory. Following the Design Science Research methodology, we develop humanoid agents based on the proposed framework and evaluate their performance using three metrics: the Turing Test, Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the decision distributions of the agents and humans in classic economic decision-making games, and the Confusion Matrix-derived Metrics. The findings show that humanoid agents designed using the proposed framework exhibit a higher degree of human-like behaviors than baseline agents. This paper contributes to the design of humanoid agents and the development of cognitive architecture in the following ways. First, it introduces a novel framework for designing humanoid agents in economic decision-making, integrating cognitive architecture and dual-process theory. Second, it incorporates a reasoning module based on dual-process theory into traditional cognitive architecture, empowered by LLMs, thereby expanding the design and application potential of cognitive architecture.

Title: Exploring the involuntary and excessive use of mobile instant messaging for work-related purposes: A triangulated mixed-methods investigation
Authors: Tingting Hou, Ping Ding, Keke Hou, Yifeng Ruan, Xin (Robert) Luo
Abstract: While mobile instant messaging (MIM) has become increasingly ubiquitous in professional settings, its psychological implications remain underexplored. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and the stressor-strain-outcome framework, the present study examines how involuntary use and excessive use of MIM are associated with social media fatigue and switching intention. Employing a three-stage mixed-methods design comprising an initial qualitative exploration, a quantitative study, and a qualitative follow-up, this study identifies four context-specific psychological states: privacy concerns, information overload, impaired autonomy, and work-to-life conflict. The findings reveal that these psychological states underlie the associations of both excessive and involuntary MIM use with user fatigue and switching intention. These insights illuminate the nature of technology-induced digital stressors in contemporary work environments.

Title: Breaking the spiral of silence in social media: The interplay between opinion climates and hardcore user identity
Authors: Wanghao Dong, Weijun Wang, Wenjing Zhong, Yu Tong, Wei Wang, Chunmei Gan
Abstract: Social media comment sections (SMCSs) have emerged as important venues for public opinion formation. However, whether the presence of hardcore users (who persistently express minority views) can mitigate conformity pressure, and how the identity (ordinary user vs. opinion leader) further moderates this effect, remain largely unexplored. Drawing on spiral of silence (SoS) theory, a preliminary study and three online experiments were conducted within a simulated SMCS environment, systematically manipulating the opinion climate (supportive, opposing, or neutral), the presence of hardcore users, and their perceived identity. Repeated-measures ANOVAs indicated that a dominant opinion climate drives attitudinal alignment toward the majority position, consistent with the SoS mechanism. However, hardcore users perceived as ordinary members exerted no significant buffering effect. Crucially, when hardcore users were identified as opinion leaders, they effectively disrupted the conformity process, preventing majority-consistent attitude shifts. Theoretically, these findings extend the SoS theory to information-system-mediated environments by identifying opinion leader identity as a critical boundary condition for the spiral mechanism. Practically, the results offer actionable insights for platform design and content moderation strategies aimed at fostering viewpoint diversity and countering opinion homogenization in online discourse.

Title: Explaining the Violation of Non-Disclosure Agreements by Software Developers
Authors: Gregory D. Moody, Mikko Siponen, Merrill Warkentin, Weijie Zhao
Abstract: Competition among software firms has given rise to theft of intellectual property and numerous patent infringement lawsuits. A potential key threat is the unauthorized use of code, ideas, or program components by competitors. If former employees or outsourcing partners steal their employers’ intellectual capital, organizations’ software product development may be compromised as a result. This unauthorized use of previous employers’ intellectual capital is a violation of non-disclosure agreements (NDA) by software developers , but IS research has offered limited explanation of this phenomenon. As a first step in addressing this gap, we present a model explaining NDA violations based on the social learning theory (SLT) of criminology. The new insight derived from SLT focuses on the motivations for violation, rather than on how organizations can deter such violations, which is the dominant theoretical lens in IS security to address information policy violations. We argue that, owing to the inconspicuous nature of NDA violations, deterrence (theory) alone is insufficient to explain such behavior. Our empirical findings show that deterrence mechanisms (e.g., formal sanctions and whistleblowing expectations) significantly but modestly reduce violation intentions, whereas social-learning mechanisms, especially significant others’ influence and perceived benefits, have stronger effects. These findings highlight the need to understand software developer culture and the social influences, which affect developers’ motivations to abide by the NDA.

Title: Exploring the practice of business support in resource-constrained contexts
Authors: Elias Osei, David Sarpong, Derrick Boakye, George Ofosu
Abstract: Abstract Despite extensive investment in entrepreneurial support organisations (ESOs), ostensibly similar support arrangements often generate markedly different outcomes for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs). Existing research explains support through programme architectures, governance arrangements, network structures, and performance outcomes, yet offers limited insight into how support is actually accomplished in everyday practice, particularly in resource-constrained environments characterised by institutional fragmentation and limited organisational slack. Drawing on the recent turn to practice in contemporary social theory, this study examines how business support becomes workable under such conditions. We analyse 58 interviews with scientists, technology transfer officers, policymakers, financiers, and entrepreneurs across six ESOs in the Global South, complemented by observations and documentary evidence. Our findings identify four interrelated organising practices through which support is accomplished: parsing resource needs, entrepreneurial framing of academic work, prioritising appropriate technologies, and orchestrating relational ties. Rather than operating as discrete interventions, these practices function as mutually reinforcing accomplishments through which actors align materials, meanings, and competencies in situ. We contribute by re-theorising business support as a situated organising accomplishment rather than a programmatic intervention, organisational capability, or support architecture. This perspective opens the black box of support enactment, explains why ostensibly similar support arrangements generate heterogeneous outcomes, and reveals how resource constraints actively shape the forms of organising through which support becomes workable. In doing so, we extend scholarship on ESOs and technology transfer while offering practitioners a diagnostic vocabulary for strengthening support under conditions of constraint.

Title: The contingent value of business incubation: temporal dynamics and incubator quality
Authors: Diogo Costa Almeida, Ana Maria Soares, Fernando Belezas, Paulo Afonso, Luís Pinto Ferreira
Abstract: Although business incubators are one of the main public policy instruments for promoting entrepreneurship and regional development, after nearly 30 years of research, there is still no consensus on their value, with several studies presenting contradictory findings on the performance of incubated companies. A review of the previous literature identified several methodological biases that may overestimate the outcome of these organisations. In a robust approach, this study paired a total of 442 incubated companies, spread over four periods, during and after incubation, with a corresponding sample of non-incubated twin companies. The association between incubation and performance was tested on a total of five metrics. The influence of the type of incubation (physical vs. virtual) and the quality of the incubator was also analysed. The results show that the performance advantage associated with incubation is not absolute but contingent, depending on the period of analysis and the quality of the incubator. Specifically, positive associations are concentrated during the first three years of incubation but dissipate in the post-incubation period. High-quality incubators are associated with positive performance outcomes, whereas for low-quality incubators, no evidence of such positive associations is found. Combined with the methodological biases identified, these results provide empirical grounding for future research aimed at reaching a clearer consensus on the specific circumstances in which the association with incubators is positive and when it is not.

Title: When specialists survive: rethinking niche width, capability fit, and adaptation in a declining craft industry
Authors: Şükrü Özen, Serkan Dirlik
Affiliations: Izmir University of Economics, Business Administration Department, Sakarya Cd., No. 156 Balçova, Izmir 35330, Türkiye . e-mail: ozen.sukru@ieu.edu.tr; Muğla Sıtkı Koçman University, Department of Business Administration, Kötekli Kampüsü, Muğla 48000, Türkiye . e-mail: sdirlik@mu.edu.tr
Abstract: Abstract We examine how generalists and specialists adapt under coarse-grained changes. Analyzing a declining copperware cluster, we develop a grounded model of form-dependent adaptation, linking ecological fit, capability fit, and organizational alignment. Specialists faced greater ecological misfit but redeployed broadly and narrowly valuable capabilities into decorative markets, where lower redeployment costs and stronger capability fit enabled related diversification. Organizational alignment then sustained diversification. Extending the niche width-adaptability debate to declining craft industries, the study reveals context-dependent dynamics overlooked in prior research.

Title: Confirmation or overload? The nonlinear impact of topic-extension on revisiting consultation in online healthcare
Authors: Jiantong Zhang, Yuting Zhang, Binhua Ye, Yushan Guo
Abstract: Sustaining patient engagement remains a central challenge for online health communities (OHCs). This study examines how physicians' topic-extension responses—the proactive provision of clinically relevant information beyond patients' explicitly stated inquiries—shape revisiting consultation and through which mechanisms. Using a multimethod design, Study 1 analyzes physician-period consultation data from a leading OHC and reveals an inverted U-shaped relationship between topic-extension and aggregate revisiting consultation: moderate extension increases revisiting, whereas excessive extension reduces it. This nonlinear relationship becomes flatter when physicians serve patient populations with higher health literacy. Study 2 employs a scenario-based experiment to establish causality and unpack the underlying psychological process. The results show that increasing topic-extension from a low to a moderate level enhances revisiting intention through greater expectation confirmation, whereas increasing it from a moderate to an excessive level reduces revisiting intention through heightened perceived cognitive load. Together, the findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of topic-extension responses depends on both the extent and the characteristics of the patient population and provide important implications for optimizing online physician–patient communication.

Title: Institutionalizing portfolio entrepreneurship: the Venture Studio model
Authors: Davide Viglialoro, Giuliano Sansone, Elisa Ughetto, Paolo Landoni, Martin Lukeš
Abstract: Venture Studios (VSs) are organizations that create start-ups by acting as founders or co-founders and operating through standardized venture creation processes conducted in parallel. To examine this organizational model and delineate its distinctiveness from others, we developed a global database, conducted multiple case studies with twelve European VSs and two international networks, and administered a worldwide survey. Drawing on human capital and organizational learning perspectives, this study identifies the architectural characteristics and mechanisms through which VSs institutionalize portfolio entrepreneurship. Our findings reveal how VSs convert individual entrepreneurial expertise into organizationally codified human capital. In doing so, VSs extend entrepreneurial agency and cognition from individuals to organizations, offering an organizational model for parallel venture creation. Finally, we clarify how VSs complement other entrepreneurial actors by reducing early-stage uncertainty and generating validated, investment-ready ventures.

Title: Neurosymbolic Large Language Models: A Survey of Symbolic Integration, Reasoning and Explainability
Authors: Maneeha Rani, Bhupesh Kumar Mishra, Dhavalkumar Thakker
Abstract: Abstract LLMs have demonstrated strong language-learning and human-like response-generation capabilities, and they are increasingly used to support decision-making in high-risk sectors. However, their internal decision processes remain difficult to interpret, and their responses may lack transparency. The literature has explored numerous approaches to address transparency challenges in LLMs, including Neurosymbolic AI (NeSy AI). NeSy AI approaches were primarily developed for conventional neural networks and may not transfer directly to the distinctive characteristics of LLMs. Consequently, there is a limited systematic understanding of how symbolic AI can be effectively integrated into LLMs. This paper aims to address this gap by first reviewing established NeSy AI methods and then proposing a novel taxonomy of symbolic integration in LLMs, along with a roadmap to merge symbolic techniques with LLMs. The taxonomy organises the literature across four dimensions: (1) the stage of LLM development at which symbolic information is integrated; (2) the coupling mechanism; (3) the architectural paradigm; and (4) the algorithm-level or application-level perspective. The review identifies commonly used benchmarks, recent advances and important research gaps, and uses these findings to outline directions for future research. By highlighting the latest developments and notable gaps in the literature, it offers practical insights for implementing frameworks for symbolic integration into LLMs to enhance transparency.

Title: A Multi-Dimensional View of IS Discontinuance: Insights Using Socio-Technical Systems
Authors: Smit Ghelani, Vidushi Pandey
Abstract: Information Systems (IS) discontinuance is an increasingly relevant phenomenon as individuals and organizations continuously reassess their engagement with technology. Research on IS discontinuance has examined this phenomenon across social media, consumer applications, and organizational systems, but the findings remain dispersed across contexts and levels of analysis. This review analyses 97 studies qualitatively using the Gioia method and synthesizes evidence using Leavitt’s socio-technical systems (STS) framework. The analysis identifies drivers and inhibitors across four dimensions: People, Technology, Task, and Structure. It further shows how interactions among these dimensions shape intermittent discontinuance, replacement, and permanent discontinuance. By integrating insights from diverse IS contexts, this review presents discontinuance as a multidimensional process shaped by socio-technical interdependencies rather than a single decision. The findings highlight key theoretical directions for IS discontinuance research and provide practical implications for system designers, organizations, and policymakers managing digital transitions.

Title: R&D Internationalization and Its Impact on Green Innovation: An fsQCA‐Based Comparison of Global R&D Divisions and Subsidiaries
Authors: Xinyi Gao, Cheng Liu, Siyuan Dong
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management Fuzhou University Fuzhou China; School of Economics and Management Anhui Agricultural University Hefei China; School of Business Ludong University Yantai China
Abstract: ABSTRACT We examine the role of R&D internationalization in green innovation among Chinese firms based on two organizational modes of Chinese firms in Belt and Road (B&R) countries, which are overseas R&D divisions and overseas R&D subsidiaries. Based on institutional theory and dynamic capability theory, we examine how the external drivers (policy support, regulatory environment, market norms) interact with internal drivers (sensing, integration, reconfiguration, innovation). We find the configurations that would result in green innovation in various organizational structures using fuzzy‐set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). There are four different models of green innovation. Policy sensing‐driven and regulatory integration‐driven green innovation models are mainly observed in overseas R&D divisions, whereas market reconfiguration‐driven and market innovation‐driven green innovation models are mainly observed in overseas R&D subsidiaries. Our findings extend the literature on R&D internationalization and green innovation by showing that the effectiveness of institutional and capability drivers depends on organizational form and by identifying multiple configurational pathways through which international R&D units achieve green innovation.

Title: From creative output to creative governance: Legitimizing AI-generated creativity under deepfake uncertainty
Authors: Domitilla Magni, Giuseppe Lanfranchi, Maria Esmeralda Palaganas
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence challenges established foundations of innovation legitimacy by decoupling output quality from human effort, intention, and responsibility. When creative outputs no longer provide reliable signals of human agency, legitimacy judgments must be reconstructed through alternative interpretive cues. This study reconceptualizes innovation legitimacy as an inferential process formed under conditions of technological opacity and examines how governance practices shape legitimacy judgments in AI-mediated creativity. Drawing on a survey-based experiment (N = 240), we investigate how configurations of AI involvement, transparency timing, and deepfake-related manipulation cues influence perceived deception, perceived human effort, and perceived authenticity. Legitimacy judgments, operationalized as inferential assessments of deception, effort, and authenticity, are distinguished from their downstream attitudinal and behavioral consequences. The findings show that legitimacy in AI-mediated creativity shifts from output-based evaluation toward governance-dependent sensemaking. Transparency operates as an interpretive mechanism whose effects depend critically on timing, while deepfake cues systematically heighten moral uncertainty and undermine legitimacy. By specifying the microfoundations through which legitimacy breaks down and is partially reconstructed under AI-induced opacity, the study advances innovation theory by reframing legitimacy as a governance-dependent inferential achievement. This reframing differs from existing interpretive and institutional accounts: governance is conceptualized not as a mechanism that generates legitimacy directly through compliance or ceremonial conformity, but as an interpretive infrastructure that shapes the conditions under which audiences can form legitimacy judgments when conventional output-based cues are absent. The findings contribute to debates on AI governance, innovation diffusion, and responsible innovation in contexts characterized by ambiguous agency and uncertainty about algorithmic production processes.

Title: Frugal business models: A systemic perspective from the international literature
Authors: Ana Paula Provin, Ademar Dutra, José Baltazar S.O. A. Guerra, Ana Regina de Aguiar Dutra, Anelise Leal Vieira Cubas
Abstract: Frugal business models have emerged as innovative alternatives for serving low-income markets through affordable, sustainable, and robust solutions, supporting organizational strategies under conditions of resource constraints. Initially developed in the context of emerging economies, these models have increasingly gained relevance in developed countries as well, driven by growing concerns regarding resource efficiency and sustainable consumption. Despite the rising academic interest in frugal innovation, research on frugal business models remains fragmented, with limited consolidation of their defining characteristics, dominant patterns, and broader impacts. To address this gap, this study conducts a systematic literature review using the ProKnow-C method. The analysis of a final portfolio of 74 articles identified 23 illustrative cases of frugal products and services and enabled the mapping of recurring patterns, strategic logics, and challenges associated with frugal business models. The findings indicate that these models can support sustainable innovation strategies; however, further empirical research is required to assess their impacts across both emerging and developed market contexts. Overall, this study contributes to the literature by synthesizing existing knowledge and outlining avenues for future research in this domain.

Title: From approval to routine use: the two-stage technology transfer of new drugs in U.S. clinical practice
Authors: Yuchen Wang, Giedre Kvedaraviciene, Phillip Phan
Abstract: Regulatory approval transfers a new drug’s availability to clinical practice, but not its routine use. We study the early diffusion of five drugs approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2015, Tresiba, Entresto, Corlanor, Orkambi, and Uptravi, spanning diabetes, heart failure, cystic fibrosis, and pulmonary arterial hypertension, as a technology transfer process, using linked Medicare Part D prescription events, beneficiary and outpatient claims, and prescriber characteristics over a four-year post-marketing window. We model diffusion as a two-stage process. A prescriber-level survival model of adoption timing, in which non-adopters are retained as right-censored observations, and a model of prescribing intensity conditional on adoption. The first stage is systematic, where patient-mix, prescriber, drug-attribute, and geographic covariates discriminate adoption timing well, although which factors matter, and in which direction, are heterogeneous across products. The second stage is not. The same covariates leave most of the variation in intensity unexplained. Patient-level treatment histories show that adoption is narrow but durable. Most Tresiba initiators with recent comparator exposure discontinued the comparator, while most Entresto initiations were new starts, and median persistence exceeded 600 days for both drugs. Yet, their adoption remained concentrated in a limited number of patients per adopting prescriber, and no S-shaped diffusion curve appears within four years. Consistent with Gort and Klepper ( 1982 ), this departure from the S-curve may reflect physicians’ thin accumulated experience with newly launched drugs as much as deliberate risk management. We draw implications for diffusion theory, launch strategy, and health policy.

Title: Too old for TikTok? Nope! Exploring senior adult viewer’s short-form video platform addiction through attachment theory and socio-technical framework
Authors: Zhenya Robin Tang, Xueyan Dong, Yuxin Tian, Dahui Li
Abstract: The rapid proliferation of short-form video platforms (SVPs) has fundamentally reshaped the digital media ecosystem, engaging users from diverse demographic backgrounds. Contrary to popular belief, older adults are not immune to the allure of SVPs, with a growing number of older users becoming addicted to these platforms. Drawing on attachment theory and socio-technical perspective, this study developed a research model to examine the factors driving SVP addiction among senior adult users. Our results indicate that social factors (lack of entertainment channels) and technical factors (perceived functionality complementarity and perceived recommendation personalization) influence senior adult users’ SVP addiction through emotional attachment with content creators and functional attachment with SVP. The findings of the current study offer implications for theory development in the fields of social media addiction and technology use among older adults as well as practical suggestions for promoting the mental health and well-being of older adults in the digital age.

Title: Government institutions and data custodianship over personal information: Comparing citizen preferences in Hong Kong and South Korea
Authors: Jung Eun Kim, Kwan Nok Chan, Wai Fung Lam, Edward Kei Fung Chan
Abstract: Public administration researchers traditionally approach the use of personal information in public service through the lens of direct user control, but a combination of cognitive constraints and rapid digitization has made privacy-preserving choices exceedingly difficult for citizens to manage independently. Recent research has shifted toward the notion of “data custodianship”, where public institutions serve as custodians of personal information. In a survey experiment conducted in Hong Kong ( n = 1031) and South Korea ( n = 1040), citizens evaluated their trust in various institutions serving as custodians tasked with managing biometric information for facial recognition. The findings suggest that while institutional trust can be influenced by accountability mechanisms, it is also shaped by individuals' experiences with public institutions, as well as their political orientation, social trust, and privacy preferences. Trust in one functional domain of data custodianship—such as data collection—may not carry over to others, like storage or management. Custodianship is only viable as a policy alternative to user control in data-intensive solutions if its design accounts for variation in public trust across societies, individuals, and aspects of data governance.

Title: Digital resilience in delivering public services. A conceptual model
Authors: Katarzyna Sienkiewicz-Małyjurek
Abstract: Digital resilience has gained increasing attention as public organizations face accelerating digital transformation and growing social threats. However, research remains fragmented, providing limited understanding of how digital resilience develops in public service delivery and how its determinants relate to its manifestations. This study addresses this gap by conceptualizing digital resilience from an organizational perspective and examining the relationships between its determinants and manifestations in public service delivery. The analysis draws on 59 semi-structured interviews conducted in Poland, a relevant setting due to its advanced public-sector digital transformation and exposure to multiple contemporary crises. Using thematic analysis and the Gioia methodology, the study identifies three manifestations of digital resilience: continuity and availability of public services, organizational development, and technologization of internal and external processes. It further reveals four determinant groups: social, technological, organizational, and legal. The findings show how these determinants jointly enable and shape the identified manifestations, resulting in different resilience outcomes in public service delivery. Building on these relationships, the study develops a stakeholder-driven conceptual model and proposes a definition of digital resilience. The study contributes to digital governance research by offering conceptual clarity and an integrated framework that explains how digital resilience develops in public service delivery.

Title: Can Larger Language Models Always Perform Better? A Comparison of GPT, FinBERT, and Dictionaries in Evaluating Management Sentiment
Authors: Xu Yang, Peng Liang, Indranil Bose, Nan Hu
Abstract: Management sentiment analysis is a foundational yet domain-intensive task in information systems (IS) research, requiring substantial domain knowledge to be measured reliably. Domain-specific models emphasize specialization by embedding knowledge through extensive pretraining and fine-tuning, whereas general-purpose large language models (LLMs) rely on few-shot learning to achieve broad generalization across tasks. In this study, we investigate the extent to which general-purpose LLMs, without domain specialization, can capture managerial sentiment. We conduct a series of experiments to evaluate the performance of a general-purpose LLM (GPT-3.5) relative to a domain-specific model (FinBERT) and a traditional dictionary-based approach in classifying managerial sentiment from MD&A disclosures. These findings reveal a non-linear pattern of model performance: GPT-3.5 substantially outperforms the dictionary-based approach, while FinBERT achieves slightly higher accuracy than GPT-3.5. These findings show that larger-scale general-purpose LLMs do not uniformly dominate smaller domain-specific models and highlight the importance of model-task alignment in domain-intensive IS contexts.

Title: A review on blockchain-driven e-healthcare service user empowerment
Authors: Anjali Shishodia, Rohit Sharma, Angappa Gunasekaran, Prikshat Verma
Abstract: This paper aims to conduct a hybrid study focusing on blockchain-driven healthcare service user empowerment and its applications in e-healthcare concepts, using bibliometric, network, thematic, and content analyses. The study considered 778 published articles from 2016 to 2024 and conducted a network analysis of the 49 most-cited articles in the domain of blockchain-driven healthcare service user empowerment. The results underscore the underlying research areas, which are further clustered into five major principles, namely, data ownership and control, data privacy and security, trust and transparency, incentivization and engagement, and accessibility and equity. The results offer unique insights for theoretical and managerial implications and propose a conceptual framework for future study in this sector.

Title: Mental Health Support for People with Depression Using Artificial Intelligence: The Effects of Appearance and Emotion Anthropomorphism
Authors: Jingjing Tong, Wenjing Chen, David Jingjun Xu
Abstract: Depression is globally prevalent, yet psychiatric shortages restrict care access. Artificial intelligence (AI) doctors may address this shortage, but their adoption is hindered by distrust and privacy concerns. By making AI doctors seem socially present and humanlike, anthropomorphic design may shape users’ psychological responses. Drawing on media equation theory, this study distinguishes between appearance and emotion anthropomorphism and examines their effects on trust, privacy concerns, and adoption intention, with perceived public stigma as a moderator. A 2 × 2 experiment with 319 participants showed that emotion anthropomorphism increased trust and reduced privacy concerns, whereas appearance anthropomorphism had no significant effects. Trust increased adoption intention, whereas privacy concerns reduced it. The two designs showed negative interaction effects: each effect weakened when the other design was high. Emotion anthropomorphism’s effects were stronger under high perceived public stigma. This study advances AI anthropomorphism research and guides AI doctor design.

Title: AI advice and human metacognition
Authors: Leily Soleimanof, Derrick Neufeld
Abstract: Although organizations increasingly rely on artificial intelligence (AI) to support decision making, research consistently finds that decision makers exhibit varied responses to algorithmic advice. While prior research has examined when users are more likely to accept or reject AI advice, little is known about the cognitive factors associated with these responses or the broader psychological consequences of working with AI. Drawing on metacognition theory, this study explores how individuals monitor and revise their judgments when confronted with algorithmic advice in a behavioral experiment with 440 participants. The results indicate that metacognitive estimates of confidence are strongly associated with responses to algorithmic advice. However, individual differences in metacognitive sensitivity shape how consistently they rely on confidence when responding to AI advice. Specifically, when metacognitive sensitivity is low, confidence judgments are based on noisy internal states, which, in turn, lead to inconsistent patterns of advice-taking. We also find that exposure to contradictory AI advice is associated with lower retrospective confidence in individuals' subsequent decisions. This loss of confidence is more pronounced when individuals reject the AI advice, highlighting a hidden psychological cost of advice rejection. These findings contribute to the growing body of information systems (IS) research on algorithmic advice-taking by demonstrating that effective human-AI collaboration requires not only improvements in system design but also fostering users' metacognitive sensitivity.

Title: The impact of generative AI on news believability: A mind perception perspective
Authors: Yang Liu, Junming Zeng, Shan Liu, Lu Han
Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into news production, concerns have emerged about its impact on audience trust and news believability. Drawing on mind perception theory, this study investigates how perceived attributes of the news producer's mind, namely, cognitive ability, emotional ability, and intentionality, mediate the relationship between the type of news generator (AI vs. human) and news believability. We adopt a multi-methods approach, combining an empirical analysis of news videos and user comment data from Douyin with two controlled online experiments to uncover the psychological mechanisms. Results reveal an AI trust penalty: AI-generated news is perceived as significantly less believable than human-generated news, primarily because of lower attributions of cognitive and emotional abilities, as well as heightened perceptions of manipulative intent associated with AI news generators. However, this effect varies across evaluative contexts. The AI trust penalty is attenuated in hard-news contexts, compared with soft-news contexts, where audiences evaluate believability through diagnostic content-based cues such as factual accuracy and evidentiary support. It is also attenuated in belief-consistent contexts, where belief alignment activates an automatic acceptance process that reduces scrutiny of the news generator. These findings contribute to research on trust in AI-generated content, mind perception, and news consumption by identifying the specific mental attributes audiences consider when evaluating news and by delineating the boundary conditions under which mind attribution is more or less likely to occur. We conclude by discussing practical implications for AI involvement and disclosure strategies in news production.

Title: Actualized fitness technology affordances: Conceptualization and validation of a measurement scale
Authors: Yafang Li, Michelle Carter, Robert E. Crossler
Abstract: Prior research on fitness technologies has identified numerous affordances that support users’ fitness goals. However, these affordances are often conceptualized as perceived action possibilities and described using inconsistent labels across studies, resulting in fragmented constructs and limited cumulative theorizing. Affordance actualization theory suggests that technological affordances have consequences only when enacted through users’ actions. Yet empirical measures capturing such enactments remain underdeveloped. To address this gap, we developed and validated a measurement scale for actualized fitness technology affordances. Following established scale development procedures, we generated items, refined the scale, and assessed reliability and validity through three rounds of data collection across student, MTurk, and Prolific samples. The resulting four-factor, 18-item scale captured distinct patterns of actualized affordances—self-appraisal, social appraisal, rewarding, and reminding—reflecting recurring, goal-directed actions performed through fitness technologies in practice. We found that the validated instrument extended the explanatory value of affordance actualization theory in fitness technology research and established a foundation for examining how enacted behaviors relate to user experiences, identities, and downstream outcomes across digital health contexts.

Title: Designing away technostress: Digital interface nudges, cognitive effort, and digital mindset in complex decision environments
Authors: Maximilian Valta, Christian Maier, Yannick Hildebrandt
Abstract: Complex digital decision tasks can become obstructive when interface design requires users to interpret, retrieve, and compare dispersed information under ambiguity. Although technostress research recognizes information system (IS) design as a potential mitigation lever, it remains underspecified how concrete interface-level mechanisms shape users’ stress appraisals during interaction without removing objective task complexity. We theorize digital interface nudges, which are choice architecture based interface elements that structure options and guide attention without restricting choice, as a focused IS design lever that can reduce perceived cognitive effort during decision making and in turn lower perceived hindrance technostressors. We test this argument in an online experiment in which participants complete a complex car-booking task under either a default setting digital interface nudge, a salience-framing digital interface nudge, or a control interface. Both digital interface nudges reduce perceived hindrance technostressors relative to the control, and these reductions are stronger for individuals with a higher digital mindset. The study contributes to technostress research by showing how minimal choice architecture based interface interventions can shape how users appraise complexity in structured decision interfaces without removing objective complexity from the task itself. It also extends digital nudging research from behavioral choice outcomes to stress-related perceptual outcomes and identifies digital mindset as an initial user-level scope condition that shapes the effectiveness of interface structuring.
