Title: Editorial Board
Digital platform archetypes as catalysts for circular economy innovation in technology industries
Authors: Ololade A. Shonubi
Abstract: Digital platform technologies are reshaping traditional linear value chains and are increasingly positioned as primary facilitators of circular economy implementation in electronics manufacturing. This study investigates how leading manufacturers, including Apple, Samsung, Xiaomi, and Dell, use digital platforms to support circular strategies through a comparative multi-case analysis of electronics platform archetypes. The analysis identifies two distinct digital platform archetypes. Premium integrated ecosystems, represented by Apple and Samsung, target higher-value consumer segments and emphasise component integration, lifecycle control, and tightly governed proprietary platforms. These models prioritise repair, refurbishment, and lifecycle extension within highly integrated product–service systems. In contrast, accessible ecosystem orchestrators, such as Xiaomi and Dell, promote broader participation across partners and users, focusing on asset management, service modularity, and affordability for price-sensitive consumers and business clients. The findings highlight how platform design influences circular outcomes, with governance structures, business models, and digital infrastructure needing alignment with market positioning and user needs. Overall, the paper contributes to research on digital platforms and circular business models by clarifying how platform archetypes shape pathways toward more circular electronics systems.

Title: Editorial Board
Mapping the European twin transition: an evolutionary perspective on green and digital regional development
Authors: Sina Saenger, Sebastian Losacker, Stefan Hennemann
Affiliations: Justus Liebig University Giessen; Lund University
Abstract: In this paper, we examine the twin transition of European regions in green and digital technologies using patent data from 1995 to 2020. We investigate how regions have developed comparative advantages in green or digital technologies, or in both. To analyse how these comparative advantages have evolved over time, we apply geographical sequence analysis – a method recently introduced to regional research – to explore the trajectories of regions with respect to twin transition technologies. In a subsequent step, we use regression models to explain the observed sequence patterns. Our findings indicate that regions leading in both green and digital technologies (twin leaders) first establish comparative advantages in digital technologies before developing them in green domains. This suggests that the trajectory towards a twin transition is more likely to emerge through a digital pathway rather than a green one.

Title: Adoption of circular economy innovations: the role of Artificial Intelligence
Authors: Dirk Czarnitzki, Robin Lepers, Maikel Pellens
Affiliations: KU Leuven; Leibniz-Centre for European Economic Research (ZEW)
Abstract: The circular economy represents a systematic shift in production and consumption, aimed at extending the life cycle of products and materials while minimising resource use and waste. However, achieving the goals of the circular economy presents firms with the challenge of innovating new products, technologies, and business models. This paper explores the role of artificial intelligence as an enabler of circular economy innovations. Through an empirical analysis of the German Community Innovation Survey, we show that firms investing in artificial intelligence are more likely to introduce circular economy innovations than those that do not, particularly innovations aimed at lowering production externalities such as pollution and emissions reductions. The findings of this paper underscore artificial intelligence’s potential to accelerate the transition to the circular economy.

Title: Extreme weather events and firms’ eco-innovation: the role of psychological distance
Authors: Enrique Acebo, José-Ángel Miguel-Dávila, Lizbeth Gutiérrez-Rodríguez
Affiliations: University of León; University of Salamanca
Abstract: How does exposure to extreme weather events influence firms’ eco-innovation? Drawing on Construal Level Theory, we argue that extreme weather events collapse psychological distance, transforming abstract climate change into concrete operational reality through two pathways (direct managerial cognition and indirect shifts in regional environmental concern). Using causal mediation analysis with 8,366 Spanish firms (2008–2016), we decompose the association of extreme weather episodes with eco-innovation into direct and indirect pathways, finding that the direct pathway predominates over the indirect. This relationship is strongest among small, lower-rigidity firms. Their reaction to heat waves and dry spells is nearly twice the aggregate estimate, whereas medium and large firms show null responses. Sectoral heterogeneity reinforces this pattern; services respond through the indirect pathway, while agriculture and manufacturing respond through direct operational necessity. These findings indicate that low organisational rigidity, not mere physical exposure, shapes whether extreme weather events are associated with eco-innovation.

Title: Unleashing Artificial Intelligence and Supply Chain Automation: Enhancing Resilience in Complex Environments
Authors: Rizwan Manzoor, Gunjan Malhotra, Shradha Kapoor
Affiliations: Institute of Management Technology; Durham University
Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become increasingly critical for managing modern supply chain networks striving for automation while facing unprecedented disturbances. While previous research has focused on AI applications in parts, this study explores the systemic impact of AI supported supply chain automation on supply chain resilience in a complex supply chain environment. Using the dynamic capabilities view, AI was positioned to build the sensing capability, automation as the seizing capability, and risk management and velocity as reconfiguration capabilities leading to the outcome of “resilience”. This research provides a robust theoretical foundation for understanding how AI and supply chain automation paired together impact supply chain resilience and extends the dynamic capability view by further integrating supply chain complexity as the moderating factor to fill some critical gaps in current literature. To validate the model and test the hypothesis, this study collected cross-sectional data from the US and UK through Prolific using a standardised pre-tested questionnaire. SPSS and AMOS were used for the statistical analysis of the covariance-based structural equation modelling (CB-SEM). Additional, robustness checks such as Gaussian Copulas test were employed which further validated the results obtained. The results demonstrate that AI can be effectively mobilised through supply chain automation as it significantly influences and sequentially mediates through risk management, velocity to ultimately influence resilience. Results indicate supply chain complexity significantly moderates the resilience effects of AI supported supply chain automation i.e., AI-supported automation shows best results when there are high supply chain complexities. The study further recommends engineering managers to recognise pairing of AI with supply chain automation is crucial for exploiting AI to establish resilience.

Title: Institutional Pressures and Workforce Training in the Age of Automation: Evidence from Brazilian Companies
Authors: Andre Luiz Romano, Walther Azzolini Junior, Carlos Henrique dos Santos, Fabio Ferraco, Adrieli Caires

Title: Towards a Problem-Oriented Domain Adaptation Framework for Machine Learning
Authors: Philipp Spitzer, Dominik Martin, Laurin Eichberger, Niklas Kühl
Abstract: Abstract Domain adaptation is a sub-field of machine learning that involves transferring knowledge from a source domain to perform the same task in a target domain. This challenge commonly arises when data is obtained from multiple sources or when working with datasets that evolve over time. While recent advances offer promising methods, researchers and practitioners still struggle to determine whether domain adaptation is suitable for a given problem—and subsequently, which approach to select. This article develops a problem-oriented framework for domain adaptation through a systematic, iterative development and evaluation methodology, refined through three evaluation episodes. The framework distinguishes five domain adaptation scenarios, provides tailored recommendations for addressing each scenario, and offers practical guidelines for identifying the appropriate scenario for a given problem. Through multiple evaluation episodes, we tested the framework on both artificial and real-world datasets, as well as through an experimental study with 100 participants. The evaluation demonstrates that the framework correctly categorized all three real-world problem instances examined and significantly improved practitioners’ diagnostic accuracy in the controlled experiment. In summary, we provide clear, actionable guidance for researchers and practitioners seeking to employ domain adaptation techniques, even without specialized domain adaptation expertise.

Title: Bridging the Gap in Health Information Systems Adoption: What Healthcare Professionals Want you to Know?
Authors: Abey Jose, Maneesh Kumar, Alejandro F. Mac Cawley, Guilherme Luz Tortorella, Muhammad Fazal Ijaz, Roberto Vassolo, Manisha Kumar, Nick Rich
Abstract: Health information systems (HISs) are enhancing healthcare efficiency, but their adoption is slow due to various complex factors. Analysing concerns about HIS adoption from a first-person perspective yields a more nuanced, layered understanding of the underlying reasons. The research utilises the stages of concern (SoC) framework from the Concern-Based Adoption Model (CBAM) to explore individual perceptions and concerns about HIS adoption. The study employs a qualitative abductive research approach, using interviews with 25 healthcare practitioners to analyse the complexities of HIS adoption. The analysis reveals a spectrum of concerns aligned with stages of awareness, information, personal, operational–strategic–stakeholder management, consequences, collaboration, and refocusing. The major impediments to HIS implementation include individuals’ doubts about their personal capability, potential disruptions to existing workflows, and the absence of post-implementation evaluations. The findings highlight the need to consider diverse perspectives to ensure successful technology integration in healthcare.

Title: Integrated management for long-term performance improvement in complex systems
Authors: Robert Chapman Wood, Joel West
Affiliations: Lucas College and Graduate School of Management, One Washington Square, San José State University , San José, California 95192-0065 , . e-mail: robert.wood@sjsu.edu; School of Applied Life Sciences, Keck Graduate Institute , 535 Watson Drive, Claremont, California 91711-4817
Abstract: Abstract Considerable research has emphasized the difficulty of achieving large-scale change and performance improvement in complex systems. Neither of two standard theoretical approaches—modularity theory and complex products and systems theory—have explained how management can drive sustained progress. We address this gap by examining how Varian Medical internalized a previously decentralized cancer radiation therapy ecosystem and over multiple decades upgraded patient outcomes and financial performance dramatically. From Varian’s experience, we derive a new innovation-driven hierarchical approach and contrast it with other approaches to complex systems integration.

Title: Coopetitive portfolio configurations for product innovation: A crisp-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis
Authors: Nina Telg, Paul Chiambaretto, Anne-Sophie Fernandez, Boris Lokshin
Abstract: Firms create and manage coopetitive portfolios (i.e., alliance portfolios including competitors) to foster product innovation, as they provide access to various complementary but also compatible resources and knowledge that are essential for innovation. The presence of competitors in coopetitive portfolios can create specific synergies but also conflicts with other partners that could enhance or limit the occurrence of product innovation. To understand under which combinations of partner types in a coopetitive portfolio product innovation can occur, we use a crisp-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (csQCA) on a sample of 921 Dutch firms in the period 2010-2016. We show that alliances with competitors are complementary with customer alliances in promoting the occurrence of product innovation. In addition, our analysis reveals that when ties with universities are present in a coopetitive portfolio, suppliers must be present as well to introduce new products. Finally, we highlight that coopetitive portfolio configurations leading to product innovation vary according to the focal firm's size and industry dynamics.

Title: Teaching to learn and learning to teach: using machine training to develop artificial intelligence partners in new product development
Authors: Andrea Lipparini, Maurizio Sobrero, Korinzia Toniolo
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping how innovation is developed, and new product development (NPD) is an important domain at the centre of this shift, given its data-rich, high-uncertainty contexts. In this paper, we focus on the design and training of AI systems in which human expertise is encoded into machine models and the future scope of human and machine agency is determined. Drawing on organizational learning theory, we argue that training strategies defining who provides labels, which data are used, and how feedback is generated and reused, constitute design decisions that differ in how feedback is recursively structured, where knowledge is located, and how deeply expert judgment is codified. We develop and test three strategies, experiential, nudging, and generative, and instantiate them through computational simulations in the domain of geotechnical services for underwater exploration. We further assess the cross-context portability of the most effective strategy by redeploying the trained model in a second NPD setting. Our results show that strategies that recursively incorporate expert feedback across training cycles produce reliable, transferable models, whereas those that decouple human expertise from the training process converge prematurely on narrow solution spaces. These findings suggest that how firms structure the training of AI systems directly shapes model reliability and transferability, and provide a basis for theorizing how organizational routines, competencies, and relational forms of AI agency may develop as AI systems become embedded in NPD processes.

Title: When innovation fails: Nonlinear effects of innovation failure on trade credit and the moderating role of innovation disclosure
Authors: Lulu Lin, Huaqi Chai, Pengcheng Chen, Xiaodong Geng
Abstract: Trade credit plays a critical role in alleviating firms' short-term financing constraints, yet little is known about how firms adjust their use of trade credit in response to innovation failure. Drawing on the substitution hypothesis between bank credit and trade credit, this study examines how innovation failure, as a firm-level adverse shock, affects firms’ trade credit usage. Using panel data from 296 listed biopharmaceutical firms in China over the period 2007 – 2024, we document a significant U-shaped relationship between innovation failure and trade credit. Specifically, firms’ reliance on trade credit decreases as innovation failure rises from low to moderate levels, reaches its lowest point at moderate levels, and then increases as innovation failure becomes high. We further show that this U-shaped relationship is driven by a substitution mechanism between bank credit and trade credit. In addition, innovation disclosure strengthens the U-shaped relationship by improving information transparency and reducing uncertainty surrounding innovation outcomes. Overall, this study highlights the pivotal role of trade credit in alleviating short-term financing constraints arising from innovation failure from a supply chain finance perspective. It provides new empirical evidence and policy implications for optimizing corporate financing structures through effective supply chain relationship management.

Title: Transferring a Digital Platform Tool in Unilever: R&D Readiness to Adapt and Evolve
Authors: Khaleel Malik, Andrew James, Adam Kowalski
Affiliations: The University of Manchester; Unilever R&D Port Sunlight Laboratory
Abstract: Digital technologies are reshaping industrial research and development (R&D), yet multinational corporations (MNCs) continue to face significant challenges when transferring and embedding digital tools across globally distributed research sites. Limited research has examined how R&D engineers adapt to digital tools that alter established routines and reshape everyday work practices. This study investigates the intra-firm transfer of the Digital Manufacturing Platform (DMP) tool in Unilever, a leading global fast moving consumer goods company, focusing on its introduction from the corporate R&D center in the UK to laboratories in China and the USA. Drawing on a qualitative case study approach with in-depth interviews of process engineers and managers, the analysis indicates largely positive adoption, particularly in experimental traceability and knowledge sharing. The findings also reveal tensions that arise during the rollout, reflecting behavioural and organizational complexity associated with cross site deployment of digital tools. The study contributes to research in engineering management by identifying managerial actions that support successful technology transfer, including sustained communication and structured planning. It also emphasizes the importance of R&D engineers developing digital literacy as a key capability for interpreting and engaging with emerging technologies.

Title: How doctors’ and nurses’ work-related motivations shape perceived system benefits and resistance to CPOE
Authors: Hyoung-Yong Choi, Mark Keil, Arun Rai, Likoebe Maruping
Abstract: User resistance to information systems (IS) remains a persistent challenge, particularly in hospital environments, which are not traditional command and control organizations. Prior research on resistance to IS has primarily emphasized structural changes (e.g., in routines, power, autonomy) triggered by adopting a new IS and how such changes affect users’ perceptions (e.g., inequity, threat of job loss). Less attention has been paid to how work-related motivations are associated with users’ resistance to newly implemented systems. Drawing on an affordance-informed perspective, we examine how healthcare professionals’ work-related motivations (motivation for quality and motivation for efficiency) are associated with their appraisals of the perceived system benefits of computerized provider order entry (CPOE) and, in turn, with resistance to CPOE. Using repeated cross-sectional survey data collected from doctors and nurses across three implementation stages, we find that perceived system benefits mediate the association between motivation for efficiency and resistance to CPOE for both groups. In contrast, perceived system benefits only mediate the association between motivation for quality and resistance among nurses. We also find that the negative association between perceived system benefits and resistance is stronger for doctors than for nurses in the earlier implementation stages. This study extends IS resistance research by offering an affordance-informed explanation of how the same system may be appraised differently across occupational roles and work-related motivations in a professional healthcare context. It provides practitioners with insights into how to establish an effective CPOE implementation strategy to reduce healthcare professionals’ resistance to CPOE depending upon professional role and implementation stage.

Title: Who will generate buzz for you? Predicting review writers for local businesses and online sellers
Authors: Eunjung Lee, Yang Wang, Huimin Zhao
Abstract: Despite extensive research on electronic word of mouth, few studies predict which existing buyers will write reviews, although reviews are critical for businesses seeking online buzz. A key challenge is identifying features that link a potential reviewer to a specific product. Drawing on two ostensibly opposing social mechanisms—homophily and differentiation—we derive two review-style-matching measures that capture a consumer's tendency to bond with existing reviewers or stand out from them. Rating style matching reflects similarity between a user and a product's existing reviewers in rating tendencies, while topic matching captures similarity in the topics they discuss. We also construct measures of users’ review experience, which interact with review style matching in shaping review decisions. Predictive analytics using data from two platforms show that the proposed theory-driven features substantially improve performance relative to baseline user-level characteristics. On average, AUC increases by about 32% when the proposed features are incorporated. More importantly, the results reveal that review decisions are multi-dimensional: users can exhibit homophily in rating styles while simultaneously pursuing differentiation in topic coverage, and vice versa. Rather than a binary choice, homophily and differentiation emerge as concurrent dimension-specific tendencies. We further identify experience-based conditions under which different social strategies arise, showing that both the depth and breadth of review experience shape review decisions. These patterns extend social theories of online participation by showing that similarity-seeking and distinctiveness-seeking are not mutually exclusive but operate jointly across behavioral dimensions, and they enable more targeted identification of existing consumers as potential review writers.

Title: Intermediaries, indirect local ties, and innovation output: evidence from an interfirm R&D alliance network during the emergence of the biopharmaceutical industry
Authors: Ning Wang, John Hagedoorn
Affiliations: School of Economics & Management, Shanghai Polytechnic University, Shanghai, China; University of London
Abstract: This study explores the impact of indirect local ties on firms’ innovation output, focusing on the role of intermediaries connecting firms to their indirect partners in an interfirm R&D alliance network. Our findings reveal a positive relationship between indirect local ties and innovation output. Moreover, this study introduces a comparative approach to examine two alliance governance mechanisms, relative governance strength and relative trust. Relative governance strength as a formal governance mechanism, through equity-based vs. non-equity structures, strengthens the positive impact of indirect local ties on firms’ innovation output. Yet, relative trust as an informal, trust-based governance mechanism, through repeated vs. non-repeated partnerships, does not exhibit a significant moderating effect. These insights enhance our understanding of how firms can navigate intermediaries’ self-interested behaviour to optimise innovation output, offering practical implications for strategic alliance management in knowledge-intensive industries.

Title: Revisiting the Coopetition–Innovation Performance Nexus: A Multilevel Meta-Analytic Investigation
Authors: Rui Li, Xinnuo Xu, Kaijian Li, Shuai Feng, Xiao Hu, Asheem Shrestha
Affiliations: Chongqing University; Beihang University; Deakin University
Abstract: Although many studies have examined the relationship between coopetition and innovation performance, their findings remain inconsistent and sometimes contradictory, providing no conclusive evidence regarding this relationship. To address the ongoing debates, this study employs a multilevel meta-analysis to synthesize the fragmented findings on this relationship and introduces contingency theory to examine the contextual conditions under which coopetition is particularly beneficial to innovation performance. Based on an analysis of 64 empirical studies involving 266,263 unique samples from 2004 to 2024, our results indicate that coopetition positively relates to innovation performance. Furthermore, moderation analyses of the institutional environment (i.e., institutional support for innovation and national culture), industry effect (i.e., industry technology regime and clockspeed), and research design factors (i.e., coopetition structure and innovation novelty) provide valuable insights on the debates surrounding this relationship. Specifically, the coopetition innovation performance relationship is remarkably stronger in collectivist and low uncertainty avoidance societies, as well as in industries characterized by low tech and slow-clockspeed. We also confirm that coopetition is more effective in enhancing incremental innovation performance, when innovation performance is measured subjectively. The results remain consistent throughout robustness tests such as permutation tests and multimodel inference. This study offers one of the first meta-analytic assessments of the coopetition–innovation performance linkage, establishing a robust theoretical framework that clarifies and reconciles the mixed findings in the existing literature.

Title: Information security incidents, market valuation, and supply chain spillovers: Evidence from Chinese listed firms
Authors: Xiong Zhang, Meng Li, Qiping Wang
Abstract: Although information security incidents (ISIs) have been shown to severely degrade firm value, their propagation through supply chains remains poorly understood, particularly in emerging markets with distinctive institutional structures. This study investigates ISI spillover effects on supply chain partners in China, a critical context given China's production-oriented economy, dominant State-Owned Enterprise (SOE) sector, and rapid but uneven digital transformation. Our findings challenge Western-centric frameworks in three ways. First, we uncover the “dual nature” of supply chain partner transaction concentration; while creating baseline vulnerabilities, it also provides incident-specific protection through enhanced coordination. This protective mechanism operates only for SOEs, suggesting that institutional structures transform concentration from risk to resilience. Second, incidents originating internally generate stronger partner spillovers than external attacks, suggesting that markets interpret internal failures as signaling systematic governance weaknesses that threaten business relationships. Third, we provide empirical evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) attention amplifies spillover vulnerability, revealing how AI transitions create new cybersecurity interdependencies that increase partners’ sensitivity to ISIs. These findings extend signaling and network theories by demonstrating how institutional contexts and technological capabilities fundamentally alter cyber risk transmission mechanisms. For practitioners, we highlight that optimal cybersecurity strategies must consider supply chain partner transaction concentration and AI-specific technological interdependence—such as deep algorithmic coupling and intensive data reliance—rather than applying universal risk management principles. AI transition is accelerating globally, and our evidence that cyber risk propagation differs fundamentally across institutional contexts calls for context-sensitive approaches to supply chain cybersecurity governance.

Title: Issue Information
Patent renewals in the strategic management of intellectual property rights
Authors: Jung H. Kwon, H. Dennis Park, Shu Deng
Abstract: Firms strategically manage their intellectual property rights through patent renewal decisions. Given the high uncertainty surrounding technology and innovation management, we suggest that firms are more likely to renew patents with greater technological opportunity or those technologically relevant to their existing patent portfolio. Moreover, an interaction effect between technological opportunity and relevance exists, such that firms are more inclined to renew their patents when both conditions are present. Further, the extent to which technological relevance influences the likelihood of patent renewal is amplified when a firm’s technology portfolio is more fragmented. Analyzing a sample of 4,685 firms that made renewal decisions from 1985 to 2024 and over 1.4 million patents granted in the U.S., this study provides novel insights into the factors driving strategic technology management. Firms strategically manage intellectual property rights through patent renewal decisions. In the process of renewal, firms initially evaluate the net present value of patents, subsequently taking into account their option value. Firms are more likely to renew patents that present technological opportunity or relevance to their portfolios, particularly when their patent portfolio is more fragmented.

Title: Correction to: Introduce me to your network: temporary intermediary organizations and spatial network spillovers in entrepreneurial finance
Navigating codified, tacit and novel rules: Mapping the human-AI creativity frontier
Authors: Emmanuelle Walkowiak
Abstract: This paper examines the boundary between human and machine creativity by analysing 593 tasks across 126 occupations in the cultural and creative industries. Theoretically, we propose an evolutionary conceptualisation of creativity, structured around three rule types corresponding to retention (codified), adoption (tacit), and origination (novel) phases. Empirically, using GPT-4, we generate synthetic annotations of the semantic content of task descriptions in the Australian Skills Classification. We derive indicators of cognitive and behavioural rules within tasks and their carriers (human, AI, or hybrid human-AI) to capture creativity, and indicators of AI autonomy feasibility and efficiency potential to capture GenAI exposure scenarios. The agent-rule matching suggests a specialisation of agents in carrying defined, tacit, or novel rules, as well as two mechanisms. The first is the structured novelty effect, whereby AI autonomy feasibility is higher when defined cognitive rules combine with novel rule creation. The second is the tacit knowledge boundary, whereby tacit rules are negatively associated with AI autonomy feasibility. In our interpretation, these mechanisms reflect an efficacy logic (matching the right agent to each rule type) that differs from an efficiency logic (optimising technically feasible gain potentials). Combining both logics, we derive a simulated classification of tasks into three categories. The mixed category, involving hybrid carrier configurations, predominates (86.3%), alongside limited replacement (2.7%) and AI immune (11.0%) categories. We identify two levels of human-AI complementarity. The first lies in rule types within tasks and engages different forms of creativity (combinatorial, exploratory, transformational). The second concerns efficiency potential when performing tasks.

Title: Brokerage, power and individual innovation: When do brokers act on their structural advantage?
Authors: Martha Topete, Nathan Betancourt, Flore Bridoux, Zuzana Sasovova
Abstract: Prior research has found that brokers, those who stand between two disconnected parties, may access non-redundant information that is conducive to higher innovation. However, research has also shown that occupying brokering network positions does not systematically translate into higher innovation; in other words, brokers do not always exploit such structural opportunity. To better understand the conditions under which brokers innovate, we adopt a contingency approach and theorize that the relationship between brokerage and individual innovation is contingent on individuals’ perception of their power over alters, an important aspect of individuals’ representation of the situation they are in. Using a social network analysis at a consulting and training organization in The Netherlands, we found support for our theory: employees perceiving higher power over alters achieved higher innovation in brokering network positions than employees in these positions who perceived lower power over alters.

Title: Unpacking how integrator state-owned enterprises respond to institutional demand tensions in complex product systems innovation
Authors: Guangpei Chen, Jiang Wei, Jiaming Yang
Abstract: As hybrid organizations situated at the nexus of market and state logics, integrator state-owned enterprises (SOEs) face the daunting challenge of navigating competing institutional demands. In the process of CoPS innovation, such tensions coalesce into a persistent trade-off between legitimacy and autonomy. Drawing on an inductive multiple-case study of three large integrator SOEs operating in two representative CoPS domains in China, this study examines how these firms respond to legitimacy–autonomy tensions across different phases of CoPS innovation. We identify two response strategies, namely, aggregate projection and parallel coordination , that address goal conflicts in the goal-setting phase and means conflicts in the resource-allocation phase, respectively. Moreover, we propose a theoretical model illustrating how these mutually constitutive response strategies jointly enable integrator SOEs to secure legitimacy while preserving autonomy in achieving CoPS innovation. These findings deepen the scholars’ understanding of organizational responses to institutional demands, while also contributing to literature on CoPS innovation.

Title: The innovators scalpel: A knowledge-based view of corporate divestitures & technological performance
Authors: Killian J. McCarthy
Abstract: Knowledge is a fundamental strategic resource. While extensive research examines how firms expand their knowledge base through acquisitions, less attention has been given to how firms reshape and optimize their knowledge base through divestitures. Drawing on the Knowledge-Based View (KBV), we conceptualize divestitures as a mechanism for knowledge reconfiguration, akin to an innovator’s scalpel, which firms can use to refine their knowledge stock and enhance their capacity for technological recombination. We argue that, on average, divestitures will weaken a firm’s technological performance because they reduce the size of the firm’s knowledge base, disrupt innovation routines, and create organizational uncertainty. However, we propose that when firms divest in a way that enhances their technological, structural, and organizational focus, we argue divestitures can lead to superior technological performance. We test our hypotheses using a sample of 7,138 firm-year observations, covering 919 unique firms, in 4 high-tech industries, that announced 1,794 divestitures and filed 414,128 patent applications over a 15-year period. Our findings confirm that while divestitures generally disrupt innovation, divestitures that create focus leads to more and higher-quality innovation. In doing so, our study provides theoretical and managerial insights into how firms can use divestitures to shape their knowledge base, to sustain long-term technological competitiveness, and drive innovation performance. Importantly, our study also advances the corporate strategy and innovation literature by demonstrating that divestitures can be used as an innovation scalpel, cutting away the excess, to strengthen knowledge cohesion, flow and governance.

Title: Balancing productivity and employment in the digital age: empirical evidence from Italy’s Transition 4.0 program
Authors: Giulia Palma, Francesco Scotti
Affiliations: University of Siena; Politecnico di Milano
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between the Italian Recovery and Resilience National Plan (RRNP) funds targeting the Transition 4.0 and firm-level productivity and employment. Combining panel event studies with continuous two-way fixed effects models, we find that RRNP funds positively affect both total factor productivity (tfp) and employment. Receiving support is associated with an increase in tfp by 7% and employment by 4–5%, while a 1% rise in funding is associated with a 1.3–1.4% increase in tfp and a 0.5–0.6% increase in employment. We document substantial heterogeneity across firms operating in different sectors, with larger effects in Information and Communication Technology (ICT). Moreover, training-focused projects are associated with strong firm performance. We find significant regional variation, with more pronounced results in Northern Italy. Overall, policy effectiveness is linked to sectoral and territorial conditions, highlighting the need for differentiated, place-based industrial strategies.

Title: The impact of balance in the policy mix on firm innovation performance: A motivation–opportunity–ability perspective
Authors: Jingjing Guo, Shasha Zhou, Xinyi Ke, Victor Cui
Abstract: Combining technology-push and demand-pull instruments into a policy mix has been widely employed by policymakers to stimulate innovation. Prior empirical studies have primarily investigated the impacts of the balance between the two types of instruments within a policy mix on innovation performance at the macro or meso level, with limited attention given to the roles of micro-level policy recipients and the contexts in which policies are implemented. By integrating the motivation-opportunity-ability framework with the resource-based view and institutional theory, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of how the effectiveness of a balanced policy mix in stimulating innovation is contingent upon the internal and external contexts of policy-recipient firms. Our empirical analyses are based on a panel dataset of 77 listed firms in the solar photovoltaic industry of China from 2012 to 2022. We find that the balance between technology-push and demand-pull policy instruments within a policy mix has a positive effect on firm innovation performance. Moreover, this relationship is contingent upon firms’ internal absorptive capacity and regional institutional development, and their relative importance differs between state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and non-state-owned enterprises (non-SOEs). The moderating effect of absorptive capacity is particularly pronounced for non-SOEs, whereas the moderating effect of regional institutional development is primarily salient for SOEs. This study extends the innovation literature on policy mix by shedding light on the innovation effect of policy mix balance at the micro level and its contingencies.

Title: Mapping Impacts, Barriers, and Challenges in Scientific Collaboration
Authors: Damaris Chieregato Vicentin, Gustavo Herminio Salati Marcondes de Moraes, Bruno Brandao Fischer, Dirk Meissner, Yuan Zhou, Zhongzhen Miao
Affiliations: Faculdade de Ciências Aplicadas (FCA); National Research University Higher School of Economics; Tsinghua University

Title: Does AI Investment Improve Operational Efficiency? The Moderating Role of Organizational Slack
Authors: Lujie Chen, Ao Li, Fu Jia, Chenho Chao
Affiliations: Xi'an Jiaotong Liverpool University; Capital University of Economics and Business
Abstract: Despite growing investment in artificial intelligence (AI), many firms struggle to translate this groundbreaking new technology into consistent improvements in operational efficiency (OE). Using an unbalanced panel of 1,340 Chinese listed firms from 2019–2022, we estimate firm-level OE via stochastic frontier estimation and measure AI investment as firms' monetary commitments to AI-related fixed and intangible assets. Baseline results show a U-shaped association between AI investment and OE. Drawing on resource orchestration theory (ROT), we further show that absorbed slack—an embedded buffer that supports structuring and bundling— systematically reshapes this nonlinear payoff: at low absorbed slack, the curve resembles a localized inverted U; at moderate levels, the curvature attenuates; and at high absorbed slack, the relationship shifts to a steeper U-shape with a right-shifted turning point. In contrast, unabsorbed slack exhibits weak and inconsistent moderating effects. These results are robust to alternative specifications (including industry and year fixed effects), alternative AI measures, lagged-variable robustness tests, Lewbel type IV estimation, and alternative absorbed-slack proxies with liquidity controls. These findings clarify the role of organizational slack as a boundary condition in AI driven OE and offer managers actionable guidance for building absorbed slack and calibrating the timing and scale of AI investment to turn early drag into lasting efficiency improvements.

Title: Composite value index of design patent indicators
Authors: Grid Thoma
Affiliations: Computer Science Division, University of Camerino , Via Madonna delle Carceri 7, Camerino (MC), 62032 , . e-mail: grid.thoma@unicam.it
Abstract: Abstract Design IP protection provides firms with temporary exclusivity in appropriating the economic returns from their investments in product differentiation through external appearance. This paper contributes to the literature on the valuation of design IP rights by offering a novel empirical analysis of the value distribution of US design patents. It develops a composite value index that combines 18 design indicators regarding the quality of a patent’s prior art, the patent prosecution characteristics, and the economic impact of the patent. Patent-level regression analysis of enforcement value demonstrates that the composite index shows a satisfactory explanatory power as compared to when the indicators are considered separately. At the firm level, the proposed index is positively and significantly correlated with a firm’s market value above and beyond other knowledge and IP assets.

Title: From value creation to value appropriation: How firms exploit disruptive innovation opportunities in emerging economies
Authors: Feng Zhang, Yajing Fan, Jingjing Wang, Lei Zhu
Abstract: Although emerging economies encourage firms to create value through disruptive innovations, less is known about how firms appropriate value from these innovations. Drawing on the profit from innovation (PFI) framework, this study examines how product disruptiveness influences opportunity exploitation and how this relationship is conditioned by appropriability mechanisms and institutional forces. Based on a multi-wave, multi-informant field survey and a scenario-based experiment, we find that product disruptiveness enhances opportunity exploitation by increasing perceived differentiation and perceived attractiveness. This relationship is reinforced by informal appropriability mechanisms and political ties, but diminished by formal appropriability mechanisms and government support. These findings shift attention from value creation to value appropriation in disruptive innovation research and extend the PFI framework by showing that value appropriation from disruptive innovations depends on the fit between appropriability mechanisms, institutional forces, and disruptive innovation trajectories in emerging economies.

Title: Signal visibility and patient perception: How physicians’ prosocial behavior builds reputation in online health communities
Authors: Muneer Ahmad, Anfei Xia, Jian-Jun Wang, Xiaocong Cui
Abstract: Physicians in online health communities (OHCs) increasingly provide free articles and consultations, yet how these prosocial services contribute to physician reputation remains unclear. Drawing on signaling theory, we develop a dual-pathway model that distinguishes an attention pathway through physician visibility from a perception pathway through patient evaluations. Study 1 analyzes 21,368 physician-period observations using a cohort-specific difference-in-differences design to estimate changes in recommendation-based reputation following staggered service adoption. The adoption of free article services (FAS) and free consultation services (FCS) is followed by significant short-term reputational gains, with the estimated gains concentrated among senior physicians and those affiliated with top-tier hospitals. The results also provide evidence consistent with physician visibility as a partial attention pathway. Study 2 uses a randomized scenario experiment with 226 participants to examine the perception pathway. Both prosocial service cues increase perceived benevolence and competence, which in turn predict recommendation intention. FAS exhibits an indirect-only mediation pattern, whereas FCS combines a positive indirect effect through these trust beliefs with a negative residual direct effect. This pattern suggests that more effortful prosocial services may strengthen trust-related evaluations but also generate offsetting considerations. By distinguishing signal visibility from signal interpretation and identifying professional capital as a boundary condition, this study extends signaling theory in digital healthcare. The findings also suggest that physicians and OHC platforms should support visible prosocial engagement while clearly presenting professional credentials and service information.

Title: Understanding Virtual Assistants: A Systematic Review
Authors: Citlalli Selene Avalos-Montiel, José G. Rodríguez-García, Sonia Mendoza
Abstract: Abstract Virtual assistants have their origins in the first efforts to emulate human intelligence through systems capable of passing the Turing test. Over the years, they have evolved significantly, with Siri, introduced in 2011, being the first system explicitly recognized as a virtual assistant. Since then, the development of virtual assistants has spread to various disciplines, with the aim of assisting one or more users in various tasks, using increasingly sophisticated technologies. This article presents a systematic review, in which 34 scientific literature reviews, and surveys published between 2015 and 2025 were identified and analyzed, in order to delimit the concept of virtual assistant, its evolution and current trends, including the impact of technologies such as large-scale language models. The findings reveal a terminological ambiguity, a transition from rule-based and closed-domain implementations to Artificial Intelligence driven assistants, and the emergence of capabilities such as personalization, proactivity, context awareness, and multimodal interaction. The review also synthesizes recurring limitations and challenges reported in the last decade, highlighting patterns across domains and temporal shifts. These insights contribute to a clearer conceptualization and outline promising directions for future research.

Title: Concerto of rhetoric and images: The effect of multimodal aesthetics on customers' booking intentions in P2P accommodation
Authors: Haiwang Liu, Xiaoyun Han, Limin Xiao
Abstract: Despite the importance of aesthetics in peer-to-peer (P2P) accommodation, prior studies have neither integrated rhetoric into the multimodal information framework nor examined the synergistic or antagonistic effects between rhetoric aesthetics and image aesthetics. To address this gap, this study employs text mining and image detection techniques to operationalize aesthetics as rhetoric aesthetics and image aesthetics, with the latter further comprising cover image aesthetics and sleep space image aesthetics. Based on aesthetic arousal theory, this study uses secondary data from 20,144 Airbnb listings to construct econometric models and conducts four scenario-based experiments. The results indicate that rhetoric aesthetics has an inverted U-shaped effect on customers' booking intentions, mediated by aesthetic pleasure—that is, rhetoric aesthetics exerts an inverted U-shaped effect on aesthetic pleasure, which in turn positively influences customers' booking intentions. Cover image aesthetics enhances the inverted U-shaped effect of rhetoric aesthetics and its indirect effect, whereas sleep space image aesthetics weakens both. Post-hoc analysis shows a positive direct effect of image aesthetics on customers' booking intentions. Supplementary analysis further indicates that rhetoric aesthetics linearly increases cognitive load, and that positive emotion is lowest at a low level of rhetoric aesthetics but does not differ significantly between medium and high levels. This study advances aesthetics research in P2P accommodation, deepens the understanding of the synergistic and antagonistic mechanisms of multimodal aesthetics, and provides decision support for hosts and platform managers to optimize multimodal aesthetic information to meet customers' aesthetic needs.

Title: Navigating AI-driven technological pressure: How top management team IT readiness and strategic orientation shape data breach risk
Authors: Niaz Mohammed, Chul Woo Yoo
Abstract: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping industry practices and creating new security vulnerabilities, raising questions about the effectiveness of firms' internal risk management capabilities under heightened technological pressure. Drawing on socio-technical systems theory, we investigate how top management team (TMT) IT readiness influences firm-level data breach risk under the external technological pressure of industry AI exposure, and how firm strategic positioning shapes that response. Using a comprehensive firm-year panel dataset, we first confirm, consistent with prior research, that TMT IT readiness is associated with lower data breach risk. Building on this baseline, our central findings show that this effect is not uniform but is conditioned by the firm's technological and strategic context. The breach-reducing effect of TMT IT readiness becomes stronger in industries with higher AI exposure, and this moderating effect is itself contingent on firm strategic positioning. Specifically, the effect is more pronounced among innovation-oriented firms and less consistent among efficiency-oriented firms. These findings advance the data breach literature by identifying the boundary conditions of the well-established link between TMT IT readiness and breach risk, showing that its effectiveness amplifies under higher industry AI exposure and depends on firm strategic positioning. This study also offers practical implications for managers by highlighting the need to tailor security governance to industry-level technological pressures.

Title: A Human-Centric Framework for Fair Job Recommendation Leveraging Generative AI and Data Augmentation
Authors: Jianshan Sun, Jie Shao, Kun Yuan, Dongyang Li
Abstract: Online recruitment platforms play a critical role in enabling job seekers to access employment opportunities. However, many job seekers actively browse and apply for positions but receive little feedback, reflecting a fundamental challenge of unequal information access in digital labor markets, especially for information-disadvantaged users with sparse interaction histories and biased exposure. To address this challenge, this study proposes PA2Rec, a human-centric and generative AI enhanced framework that improves fair job information access through data-level augmentation. PA2Rec integrates a multi-attribute job filtering mechanism to construct high-quality candidate opportunity sets, leverages large language models to generate pseudo-interaction samples that expand users’ accessible opportunity space, and incorporates fairness-aware prompt tuning to mitigate systematic exposure bias. Experiments on the public Zhaopin ( https://tianchi.aliyun.com/competition/entrance/231728/information .) dataset demonstrate PA2Rec significantly improves recommendation accuracy and fairness, especially for information-disadvantaged job seekers. The results highlight the effectiveness of generative AI in augmenting information access and advancing human-centric recommendation systems in online recruitment.

Title: Why do Deepfakes Spread? A Multi-Method Study of Adoption in Utilitarian and Hedonic Deep Synthesis Technologies
Authors: You Wu, Xing Zhang, Yingzhen Feng
Abstract: Deep synthesis technology (DST), exemplified by deepfakes, raises significant ethical and legal concerns, yet users continue to actively engage with such applications even when these concerns are salient. This behavioral pattern presents a theoretical paradox: ethical risk does not uniformly suppress adoption behavior across contexts. Conventional technology adoption models such as UTAUT lack ethical constructs and may therefore prove insufficient for explaining adoption in morally contested technological contexts such as DST. Moreover, prior research has predominantly treated DST as a homogeneous category, overlooking variation across application types and the heterogeneous role of ethical factors in shaping adoption intentions. This study addresses these gaps by examining users’ adoption intentions across heterogeneous DST applications and uncovering underlying mechanisms. Integrating the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) with Hunt-Vitell ethics theory, we conducted a scenario-based survey featuring utilitarian and hedonic DST applications, encompassing function-oriented contexts (e.g., public interest communication and organizational management) and entertainment-oriented contexts (e.g., celebrity impersonation and virtual performance). A multi-method strategy combining comparative analysis and configurational analysis assessed adoption differences and identified equifinal pathways. Results reveal significantly stronger adoption intentions toward utilitarian than hedonic DST. The two adoption contexts exhibit fundamentally distinct configurational logics. Utilitarian DST adoption follows a rational-instrumental logic, with descriptive norms serving as the core condition across all configurations. Performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and technology self-efficacy also emerge as frequently recurring core conditions across multiple pathways. Hedonic DST adoption, by contrast, is governed by an ethico-normative logic, with ethical acceptability serving as the core condition across all configurations. Injunctive norms, hedonic performance expectancy, and the absence of deepfake concern appear as core conditions across several pathways. These findings demonstrate that ethical risk does not uniformly suppress adoption behavior; rather, its causal role varies systematically across application contexts. This study extends UTAUT into ethically sensitive technological domains and offers differentiated, evidence-based guidance for DST governance and context-sensitive regulatory design.

Title: Unveiling the critical role of ethical leadership in information systems security compliance research: An empirical investigation
Authors: Botong Xue, Merrill Warkentin, Xin (Robert) Luo
Abstract: In the existing discourse on behavioral information systems security, a diverse array of individual and organizational attributes has been investigated regarding the employees’ information security policy (ISP) behavior. However, ethical leadership, a pivotal paradigm profoundly associated with employees’ security behavior, has been starkly overlooked in this domain. The research unveils and examines the role of ethical leadership in influencing employees’ ISP-related behaviors. To test our hypotheses and validate the research model, we conducted a scenario-based online experiment pre-study followed by cross-sectional survey of working professionals. The findings reveal that ethical leadership significantly influences both ISP in-role and extra-role behavior, directly and indirectly, through three mediators: attitude toward security behavior (ATT), subjective norm about information security (SN), and perceived behavioral control over security behavior (BC). This research contributes to the growing streams of information security and ethical leadership literatures and offers actionable managerial suggestions on cultivating ethical leadership to enhance organizational information security performance.

Title: Adoption of ChatGPT for Learning-Related Information Access: A Comparative UTAUT2 Analysis of Turkish and Polish University Students
Authors: Ali İbrahim Can Gözüm, Artur Strzelecki, Ümit Ünsal Kaya, Murat Taşdan
Abstract: Abstract This study examines ChatGPT adoption among higher education students in Türkiye and Poland through an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) framework that also includes personal innovativeness. It compares country-specific adoption patterns across the two samples and offers a cautious contextual interpretation of the observed differences. Survey data were collected from 634 students in Türkiye and 531 students in Poland, and the proposed relationships were examined using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that the extended UTAUT2 framework was empirically useful in both samples, although the relative prominence of specific predictors differed across them. Descriptively, Performance Expectancy (β = 0.258, p < 0.001) and Personal Innovativeness showed larger coefficients in the Polish sample, whereas Effort Expectancy (β = 0.104, p < 0.01) and Social Influence (β = 0.199, p < 0.001) appeared more prominent in the Turkish sample. Price Value showed a statistically significant reversed association with Behavioral Intention in Türkiye (β = -0.187, p < 0.001), whereas the association was positive in Poland (β = 0.094, p < 0.01). Habit emerged as one of the strongest predictors in the model and was positively associated with both Behavioral Intention and Use Behavior in the two samples. Taken together, the findings suggest that ChatGPT adoption in higher education is shaped by a combination of perceived usefulness, ease of use, social and practical support, habitual use, and context-sensitive evaluations of value. The study contributes to the growing literature on generative AI in higher education by showing that the same theoretical framework can reveal different adoption patterns across two national samples, while also highlighting the need for context-sensitive implementation strategies. The findings offer practical implications for higher education institutions, educators, and policy developers seeking to support the responsible and effective use of ChatGPT.

Title: A global analysis of female innovative entrepreneurship and the role of financial development
Authors: Cecilia Alvarez-Vargas, Joan-Lluís Capelleras, Francis J. Greene, Victor Martin-Sanchez
Abstract: Drawing on feminist and institutional perspectives, this study analyses whether women are equally likely as men to engage in innovative entrepreneurship and whether the maturity of debt and equity markets strengthens women's participation. We use data from 71,888 early-stage ventures across 101 countries and show that women are as likely as men to engage in innovative entrepreneurship, once crucial individual and country-level factors are controlled for. Further, we demonstrate that both debt and equity market development positively moderate this relationship. These findings reveal that gender gaps in innovative entrepreneurship reflect structural and institutional conditions rather than intrinsic propensities and highlight the role that financial development plays in supporting female innovative entrepreneurship.

Title: LLM-powered contrastive hierarchical interest learning for cross-platform information recommendation
Authors: Datian Bi, Xue Zhang, Jingyuan Kong, Gongkun Chen
Abstract: With the widespread prevalence of multiplatform usage behaviors, cross-platform heterogeneous data offer new opportunities to alleviate cold-start and sparsity issues in recommender systems; however, they also introduce challenges, such as amplified noise, semantic heterogeneity, and negative transfer. Existing cross-platform recommendation methods often merely share user or item embeddings, thereby creating difficulties in effectively distinguishing commonalities and differences in user interests across platforms; moreover, they lack unified modeling and effective utilization of multilevel interest structures. To address these limitations, this study proposes LCHIL, a large language model (LLM)-powered contrastive hierarchical interest learning framework for cross-platform information recommendation. LCHIL leverages LLMs for cross-platform data augmentation and low-order semantic modeling on heterogeneous graphs to characterize platform-local shallow interests. It then uses a heterogeneous graph attention network to aggregate higher-order interactions and extract platform-global deep interests, while incorporating perplexity-based alignment signals and gated multimodal units to model cross-platform dynamic interests. The framework integrates hierarchical interests into a collaborative contrastive learning process to reduce redundancy and noise in heterogeneous graph information and to mitigate cross-platform transfer bias. Experiments using four real-world cross-platform datasets demonstrate that LCHIL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baseline models on multiple evaluation metrics and exhibits strong effectiveness in alleviating cold-start issues and suppressing noise.

Title: Lost in translation? Academic engagement and academic entrepreneurship in Chinese universities: a review of Chinese literature from 2017 to 2024
Authors: Emil Kristoffer Hyttel Bohmann, Jason Li-Ying
Abstract: This study systematically reviews 390 Chinese-language articles published between 2017 and 2024 to examine how Chinese universities approach academic engagement and academic entrepreneurship—the two core components of the university’s “third mission.” Although Western scholarship has extensively mapped university–industry collaboration, indigenous Chinese developments remain largely “lost in translation” due to linguistic barriers and limited cross-citation. Our review identifies key indigenous concepts—such as the transformation of scientific and technological achievements, coordinated innovation, and mixed intellectual property rights (IPR) ownership—that define China’s unique, centrally driven approach to technology transfer. We find that Chinese literature prioritizes institutional and ecosystem-level dynamics, contrasting with Western emphasis on individual-level motivations and informal networks. By synthesizing these findings into a conceptual model, this study bridges the gap between Chinese and Western research communities. It offers a more inclusive, globally balanced perspective for understanding academic entrepreneurship, highlighting how diverse institutional settings shape the translation of knowledge into economic value and providing a foundation for future comparative research.

Title: Knowledge base renewal and the dynamic selection of R&D Partners: a perspective from innovation appropriation
Authors: Delin Meng, Lan Wang
Abstract: Against the backdrop of continuous knowledge base renewal, why and how firms adjust their collaborative R&D partner relationships has become an important issue for understanding the dynamic evolution of open innovation strategies. Drawing on the theory of innovation appropriation, this study uses joint patent application data from Chinese A-share listed firms from 2003 to 2022 to systematically examine the impact of knowledge base renewal on the characteristics of collaborative R&D partner selection and its underlying mechanisms. The results show that knowledge base renewal significantly reduces the number of collaborative R&D partners, the diversity of partner types, and the geographic distance of collaboration, suggesting that firms actively contract their collaboration boundaries as their knowledge bases evolve. Further analysis indicates that knowledge base renewal strengthens firms’ attention to the protection of innovation returns and drives adjustments in collaborative relationships by reinforcing informal appropriability mechanisms and increasing the diversity of knowledge recombination. Moreover, the negative effects are more pronounced when CEOs have richer functional experience and when firms occupy more prominent structural-hole positions in innovation networks. These effects are also stronger in regions with higher levels of judicial protection for intellectual property rights and more developed socialized service systems. This study demonstrates that collaborative R&D partner relationships are not determined solely by the static characteristics of firms’ knowledge bases but are continuously reconfigured as knowledge bases evolve. By revealing the innovation appropriation logic underlying the dynamic adjustment of firms’ collaboration boundaries, this study offers a new theoretical explanation for the evolution of collaborative strategies in the context of open innovation.

Title: The Lasting Impact of the First Comment in Short Videos
Authors: Xiaochen Ma, Yangyin Lin, Qiang Ye, Hao Xia
Abstract: To examine whether early-stage social signals help explain divergent engagement trajectories beyond video content, this study investigates the lasting impact of the first comment in travel short videos. Utilizing a dataset of 499 matched pairs of cross-posted travel videos and over 400,000 comments from Douyin and Kuaishou, we employ a cross-platform differential modeling approach to reduce content-related confounding and isolate comment-dynamics effects. The findings validate a dual-pathway pattern: (1) a direct sentiment pathway, consistent with emotional contagion, in which the first comment positivity shapes subsequent comment sentiment but attenuates over time; (2) an indirect volume pathway, in which a positive first comment increases early engagement, which in turn predicts higher cumulative comment volume through a persistent herding effect. The study provides a novel lens for understanding commenting dynamics in high-velocity digital ecosystems. For tourism marketers, it suggests differentiated early-stage engagement strategies for short-term sentiment management and longer-term interaction accumulation.

Title: Beyond blind feature injection: An information foraging theory-guided deep learning framework for product recommendation
Authors: Weiyue Li, Ming Gao, Jingmin An, Bowei Chen, Jiafu Tang, Xuhui Wang, Yeming Gong
Abstract: Recommender systems significantly improve the quality and confidence of consumer decisions by alleviating information overload through streamlined retrieval, playing a vital role in e-commerce platforms. However, most recommender systems underutilize contextual information and fail to explicitly model users’ cognitive processes, leading to biased preference learning. Drawing on information foraging theory, this study adopts the design science research methodology to develop Tiresias, a framework that aligns with users’ cognitive processes by mimicking how proximal cues and foraging costs are assessed for each product. Proximal cues such as product category and affinitive relationships, and foraging costs such as behavior type, dwell time, and foraging progression, are identified and encoded as learnable features. To model the product-foraging journey, Typhon is designed as a Kolmogorov–Arnold network-enhanced differential transformer with a non-invasive feature injection mechanism. A multi-task learning objective that combines next-product prediction with auxiliary cue and cost prediction refines contextualized preference representations. Experiments on datasets show that Tiresias achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming baselines by up to 5.44%. Finally, post-hoc analysis reveals learned representation patterns consistent with dynamic preference evolution throughout the user’s product foraging journey. Methodologically, the study demonstrates how information foraging theory can guide feature selection, feature learning, and objective design. Practically, the study offers actionable insights for developing cognitive process-aware recommender systems that better support consumer decision-making.

Title: Go your own way: Managerial engagement with regional innovation ecosystems for Industry 4.0 transformation in Belgian SMEs
Authors: Anastassiya Zabudkina, Olivier Lisein, François Pichault
Abstract: While Industry 4.0 (I4.0) has led to the proliferation of policy-driven innovation ecosystems aimed at supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in their digital transformation, limited attention has been paid to how managers engage with these environments in practice. This study examines how SMEs’ managers interpret, evaluate, and mobilise external support within I4.0 Regional Innovation Ecosystems (I4.0 RIE). Drawing on 25 semi-structured interviews with managers of industrial SMEs in Belgium, we adopt a sense-making perspective to analyse engagement as an interpretive process. The findings show that managers approach these ecosystems as overlapping support mechanisms, which they evaluate in terms of accessibility and usability and enact through selective, adaptive, and sometimes reversible patterns of access and use. These findings suggest that engagement with I4.0 RIE is not driven by the availability of support alone, but by how managers interpret and position it in relation to their firms’ needs and constraints. By foregrounding these dynamics, the study offers a processual view of how SMEs engage with innovation ecosystems under digital transformation.

Title: Knowledge polycentricity and technological diversification: evidence from U.S. Metropolitan Statistical Areas
Authors: Yibo Qiao, Yingcheng Li, Yangyi Wu
Affiliations: Nanjing University; Southeast University; Wuhan University
Abstract: Existing literature on regional technological diversification has primarily viewed regions as points, while little attention has been paid to their inner spatial configurations. To address this gap, this paper investigates the impact of knowledge polycentricity on regional technological diversification. Using the USPTO patent data (1976–2020), we conduct econometric analyses on 354 U.S. Metropolitan Statistical Areas and 558 four-digit CPC technology domains. Integrating the attribute-function polycentricity framework from knowledge polycentricity literature and relatedness-complexity diversification framework from Evolutionary Economic Geography studies, we find that attribute polycentricity leads to unrelated and less complex diversification, whereas functional polycentricity triggers related and more complex diversification. The primary results still hold under instrumental variable estimation and a series of robustness checks. We contribute to Evolutionary Economic Geography literature by incorporating intra-urban knowledge polycentricity into the study of technological diversification.

Title: A new framework for industrial policy: the case of semiconductors in Japan and the United States
Authors: Yukihiro Sato, Viktória Döme, Mateus Labrunie, Carlos López-Gómez, Eoin O’Sullivan
Abstract: Abstract Interest in industrial policy has intensified in recent years, calling for renewed conceptual understanding and more robust analytical tools. However, existing industrial policy frameworks remain insufficient to capture the complexity and dynamics of contemporary industrial systems and policies. To address this gap, this study proposes a novel industrial policy analysis framework comprising four analytically distinct yet interrelated dimensions: drivers shaping policy, value-chain segments, product types, and policy instrument mixes. The framework was developed through theory synthesis by integrating key dimensions identified in prior industrial policy research and was subsequently adapted to the semiconductor sector through policy document analysis of 108 policy interventions and 22 in-depth interviews. The sector was selected due to heightened policy salience arising from geopolitical tensions and supply-chain vulnerabilities. The analytical utility of the framework is demonstrated through two empirical case studies comparing (1) Japan’s semiconductor policies pre- and post-COVID-19, and (2) Japan–U.S. semiconductor policies. The first case study reveals a marked strategic reorientation in Japan’s semiconductor policy after COVID-19, characterised by clearer policy direction, expanded interventions and larger budgets, and a broader R&D scope. The second case study identifies a strategic convergence in policy instrument choices, with both countries prioritising industrial grants to support the manufacturing segment of advanced logic chips as a core competitive domain. This study demonstrates that the proposed framework can serve as a robust analytical tool not only for systematic comparison but also for identification of opportunities and threats within national industrial systems, thereby enabling more strategic industrial policy design.

Title: “Rich-get-richer”? Platform attention and earnings inequality using Patreon earnings data
Authors: Ilan Strauss, Jangho Yang, Mariana Mazzucato
Affiliations: The Bartlett Faculty of the Built Environment, University College London , 22 Gordon Street, London WC1H 0QB , . e-mail: ilan@aidisclosures.org; Office of the DSI/NRF South African Research Chair in Industrial Development, University of Johannesburg, Auckland Park Kingsway Campus , PO Box 524, Auckland Park 2006, Johannesburg; Department of Management Sciences, Faculty of Engineering, University of Waterloo , 200 University Avenue West, Waterloo, ON N2L 3G1; Institute for New Economic Thinking at the Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford , Oxford OX1 3UQ; Oxford Martin Programme on Technological and Economic Change (OMPTEC) , Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford, 34 Broad Street, Oxford OX1 3BD; UCL Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose, The Bartlett Faculty of the Built Environment, University College London , 11 Montague Street, London WC1B 5BP
Abstract: Abstract Patreon allows content creators to monetize additional content from loyal fans. Because it offers minimal native distribution, Patreon earnings largely reflect creators’ popularity on their primary external platforms (Instagram, Twitch, YouTube, Twitter/X, Facebook, or “Patreon-only”), making them a useful proxy for platform-level algorithmic attention dynamics. Fitting power-law tails to Patreon earnings by primary platform affiliation, we find three key results. First, platforms exhibit “rich-get-richer” earnings dynamics (Barabási and Albert, 1999 Science, 286, 509–512), reflected in a Pareto exponent $\alpha \approx 2$, which is closer to concentrated capital income than labor income. Second, platforms with more concentrated earnings (lower $\alpha$) have lower mean and median earnings, and thus an eroded creator “middle class.” Third, across most platforms, $\alpha$ values decline and converge over time (based on three cross-sections: 2018, 2021, and 2024), meaning earnings become increasingly concentrated among top creators—consistent with algorithmic recommendations rising in importance. Algorithmic attention allocation is a plausible driver of these patterns, though platform-specific conversion rates and audience willingness to pay may be just as important.

Title: “Will a robo-advisor help my grandpa?”: Exploring pathways to better integrate the elderly in the era of artificial intelligence
Authors: Roxana R. Iordache, Fernando A.F. Ferreira, Neuza C.M.Q.F. Ferreira, Marina Dabić, João J.M. Ferreira
Abstract: The global aging population, particularly the increasing number of individuals over 65 in Europe, presents both significant challenges and unique opportunities. This demographic shift has sparked the rise of the Silver Economy ( i.e. , a sector focused on the production, consumption and trade of goods and services aimed at improving the lives of the elderly), increasingly driven by technological solutions such as artificial intelligence (AI). Among these technologies, robo-advisors (RAs) hold promise in enhancing the quality of life, autonomy and social inclusion for older adults. However, while the potential of AI to integrate the elderly into society is widely acknowledged, there remain substantial gaps in understanding how best to deploy such technologies. Existing literature reveals critical limitations in methodologies and a lack of comprehensive models to guide the integration of AI into the lives of the elderly. This study addresses these gaps by adopting a constructivist approach and proposing a decision-support system to guide authorities in crafting effective policies and initiatives. The system is developed with input from field experts through participatory methods, specifically the Nominal Group Technique (NGT) and the DEcision MAking Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL), within a neutrosophic framework. By doing so, the study provides a more nuanced understanding of the barriers and opportunities in using RAs for the elderly, offering both theoretical advancements and practical recommendations to improve their integration into the AI-driven future of the Silver Economy.

Title: Transient Scheduling of Dual-Armed Cluster Tools With Concurrent Processing: An MIP Model and a Fast Heuristic
